title: What We Do in the Shadows
logline: Mockumentary about four vampire flatmates in Wellington. Deadpan, heavily improvised.
overview: Vampire housemates try to cope with the complexities of modern life and show a newly turned hipster some of the perks of being undead.

jokes.text: So it's 6 PM in the night time... which is when I wake up. This is always really scary part for me.
jokes.setup: Documentary-style introduction; vampire waking up at dusk is presented as a mundane routine.
jokes.punchline: He calls waking up 'the really scary part' — the most vampire-appropriate mundane complaint imaginable, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A solid cold-open joke establishing the film's central comic conceit: vampires as mundane flatmates. The 'scary part' line is a nice inversion — a terrifying creature of the night finds waking up scary. Character-specific in that Viago is the most neurotic and domestic of the group.

jokes.text: Viago cheerfully waking his flatmates: 'Wake up! Wake up everyone! Awaken! A wakey, wakey!' interspersed with sincere commentary about liking company and having a good time with friends.
jokes.setup: We expect vampires to be brooding, solitary creatures of the night.
jokes.punchline: Viago is an enthusiastic, sociable housemate who genuinely loves the flatting experience and fusses over waking everyone up like a mother hen.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of vampire mythology against domestic cheerfulness is the film's core engine. 'A wakey, wakey!' from an immortal creature of darkness is precisely the right register. Strong character integration for Viago.

jokes.text: Deacon, asked how his night was: 'I transformed into a dog and had sex.' Viago: 'Cool!'
jokes.setup: Viago cheerfully asks 'How was your night?' in the way any flatmate would.
jokes.punchline: Deacon's matter-of-fact answer ('transformed into a dog and had sex') and Viago's breezy 'Cool!' treat something deeply bizarre as a totally normal social exchange.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. Perfect economy — six words deliver an enormous amount of comedy by collision: vampire shapeshifting + casual sexual deviance + complete social normalcy. 'Cool!' from Viago is the perfect button, refusing to engage with either the supernatural or the sexual content. The joke only works because of the flatmate-documentary framing and the established cheerfulness of Viago. Near-exemplary structure.

jokes.text: Viago walks in on Vladislav, who is apparently in a compromising/embarrassing situation mid-sleep — Viago apologizes and retreats.
jokes.setup: Viago goes room to room waking flatmates for the meeting.
jokes.punchline: He walks in on something we can only infer from his 'Sorry! Sorry!' — implying Vladislav was doing something untoward even while undead and asleep.
jokes.explanation: Classic visual comedy where the transcript withholds what the audience sees. The 'Sorry! Sorry!' reaction beat implies something mortifying without stating it. Earns its score through implication and later confirmed characterization of Vladislav as a pervert.

jokes.text: Viago opening Vladislav's door, immediately recoiling and apologizing ('Sorry! Sorry!') — clearly witnessing something disturbing or sexual.
jokes.setup: Viago is cheerfully doing his rounds to invite flatmates to the meeting.
jokes.punchline: He opens Vladislav's door and immediately has to close it, apologizing — the content unseen by the camera but clearly something Viago was not prepared for.
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary visual gag — the comedy is entirely what we don't see, letting the audience fill in the gap. Later characterization of Vladislav as 'a bit of a pervert' makes this a rewatch bonus. Works well in context, though the transcript loses most of the visual impact.

jokes.text: Viago, in Petyr's ancient horror-dungeon: 'There's a lot of stuff on the floor down here, Petyr... this seems, I don't... AH! It's a spinal column, yuck! ...I just should bring a broom down here for you if you wanted to sweep up some of the skeletons.'
jokes.setup: Petyr's room is a Nosferatu-esque chamber of ancient horror filled with bones and darkness.
jokes.punchline: Viago responds to discovering a spinal column the way you'd react to finding dirty socks, and offers to bring a broom for the skeletons — treating the charnel pit as a tidiness issue.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration — only Viago, the fussy flatmate vampire, would respond to a bone-strewn dungeon with housekeeping suggestions. The 'yuck!' is perfectly calibrated: not horror, not resignation, just mild disgust. 'Sweep up some of the skeletons' is a quotable line that earns its 8+ because it couldn't come from any other character and subverts horror atmosphere with domestic comedy almost perfectly.

jokes.text: Viago presents Petyr with a live chicken as a housewarming/appeasement gift.
jokes.setup: Viago has been nervously navigating Petyr's terrifying dungeon and trying to extend a social invitation.
jokes.punchline: He produces a chicken — the kind of offering you'd bring an ancient demonic creature if you were also a considerate neighbor — completing the portrait of Viago as the ultimate vampire house-mom.
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that perfectly encapsulates the film's tonal register. The chicken is the right gift — not a human victim (too on the nose) but not a casserole dish (too mundane) — it's the precise midpoint of vampiric and domestic. Good economy.

jokes.text: Vladislav: 'Is Petyr coming?' / 'Petyr's... 8000 years old. We're not going to have Petyr at the meeting.'
jokes.setup: The flatmates are gathering for a routine meeting about household chores.
jokes.punchline: Petyr's 8000-year age is cited as the reason he won't attend — not that he's terrifying, not that he doesn't speak, just that he's 8000 years old, as if this is a perfectly sufficient and self-explanatory excuse.
jokes.explanation: The delivery of '8000 years old' as a reasonable, self-evident excuse for missing a flatmate meeting is a crisp joke. It works in isolation and also retroactively recontextualizes the terrifying dungeon sequence as simply 'elderly vampire being elderly.'

jokes.text: 'We're not just pointing the finger at you, Deacon.' / 'You're a cool guy but you're not pulling your weight in the flat.' / 'Well, I'm glad to hear that I'm cool.'
jokes.setup: Viago tries diplomatic phrasing at the flat meeting, saying they aren't singling Deacon out but then immediately singling him out.
jokes.punchline: Deacon ignores the criticism entirely and latches onto the compliment ('I'm glad to hear that I'm cool'), which is both deflection and absurdly literal self-satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: Sharp character work — Deacon's response perfectly establishes him as the rebellious, self-satisfied young vampire who can't be managed. The comic engine is the contrast between Viago's anxious diplomacy and Deacon's breezy narcissism. Very well-structured three-beat exchange.

jokes.text: 'The point is Deacon that you have not done the dishes for 5 years.'
jokes.setup: An ordinary flatmate argument about not doing the dishes.
jokes.punchline: The timescale — five YEARS — reframes ordinary domestic negligence as something only immortals could achieve.
jokes.explanation: Economy is the great virtue here — one number does all the work. '5 years' is the punchline. The joke is structurally a simple escalation of a mundane complaint into vampire-time, executed with perfect deadpan.

jokes.text: Viago: 'I'm so embarrassed when people come over here.' / Deacon: 'Why does it matter?! You bring them over to kill them!'
jokes.setup: Viago frets about domestic embarrassment in front of guests.
jokes.punchline: Deacon points out the guests are murder victims — the concept of being embarrassed by a messy kitchen in front of people you're about to kill is the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Deacon's line is a genuinely good joke — it's the film's core conceit (domestic normality vs. lethal predation) expressed in a single perfectly-constructed counter-argument. It also works as character comedy: Deacon is the one who cuts through the domestic theatre with brutal vampire pragmatism. The setup from Viago's social anxiety is well-earned.

jokes.text: 'Vampires don't do dishes.' / 'Some vampires do.' / 'Well, not serious ones!'
jokes.setup: Argument about whether vampires should be expected to do housework.
jokes.punchline: The concept of 'serious vampires' who are too serious to do dishes — delivered with complete conviction as a point of vampire identity and pride.
jokes.explanation: 'Not serious ones!' is a quotable, economical punchline. The idea that vampire seriousness is incompatible with domestic chores is a funny articulation of the film's central absurdism. Deacon owns the line perfectly as the too-cool-for-chores young vampire.

jokes.text: Talking-head about Deacon: 'Deacon's like the rebellious young vampire. He's always doing crazy things. Saying crazy things... He's just like the young, bad boy of the group.'
jokes.setup: Confessional camera reaction to the flat meeting argument.
jokes.punchline: Viago describes a centuries-old vampire as a 'young bad boy' with the slightly weary, slightly admiring tone of a parent talking about a difficult teenager.
jokes.explanation: Functional confessional comedy establishing Deacon's archetype. The irony of an immortal vampire being described in teenager tropes is mild but consistent. Not exceptional, but serves the film's character-building work.

jokes.text: Deacon's origin story: being dragged into a dark dungeon, bitten to the point of death, forced to drink foul blood — leading to: 'And it was Petyr. And we're still friends today.'
jokes.setup: Deacon narrates a genuinely terrifying sequence of abduction, near-death, and forced transformation.
jokes.punchline: 'And it was Petyr. And we're still friends today.' — the horrors are reframed as a meet-cute origin story between flatmates.
jokes.explanation: One of the best-structured jokes in the reel. The setup is an earnest, escalating horror narration — wings, screeching, forced blood-drinking — and the punchline deflates it entirely with the reveal that this terrifying creature is just their ancient flatmate Petyr, and 'we're still friends today.' The misdirection is excellent: we expect a dramatic revelation, not a cheerful social footnote. 'And we're still friends today' is quotable and earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Viago praises Vladislav at the flat meeting: 'Vlad, you are great. You put out the recycling. Which was really cool. And! The other day, I dragged a man's body down the hallway, and noticed that there was no dust. Like, I kind of... I kind of swept the hallway.'
jokes.setup: Viago balances his criticism of Deacon by praising Vladislav's contributions.
jokes.punchline: The praise is for recycling and incidentally sweeping the hallway while dragging a corpse — the murder and domestic maintenance are presented as equally mundane achievements.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the casual equivalence: recycling and body-dragging presented as equally noteworthy household contributions. 'I kind of swept the hallway' as an accidental byproduct of corpse-dragging is a sharp piece of dark comedy. The hedging ('like, I kind of...') makes it funnier by implying Vladislav isn't sure if it counts as a chore.

jokes.text: Confessional about Vladislav: 'He's a really great guy. A bit of a pervert.' / Vladislav: 'We should get some slaves!'
jokes.setup: Viago gives a warm confessional about Vladislav surviving the ages with 'it together.'
jokes.punchline: Undercut first by 'A bit of a pervert,' then immediately illustrated by Vladislav's non-sequitur demand for slaves.
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke with tight construction. 'A bit of a pervert' as a mild caveat about a medieval vampire is funny on its own; cutting to Vladislav demanding slaves is a perfect button that confirms the character note while escalating it. Character-specific — only Vladislav would say this.

jokes.text: Vladislav shows the documentary crew his torture chamber. 'I don't come in here often anymore. I was tempted to torture when I was in a bad place.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav gives a tour of his torture chamber.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't come in here often anymore. I was tempted to torture when I was in a bad place.' — torture chamber framed as a past vice or addiction, like someone who used to drink too much.
jokes.explanation: Superb deadpan. The language of recovery and self-improvement ('I was in a bad place,' 'I don't come in here often anymore') applied to mass torture is a brilliant reframing. It makes Vladislav sympathetic and monstrous simultaneously and the mundane delivery of the character sells it completely. High character integration — this is very specifically Vladislav's voice.

jokes.text: 'My thing was, I would poke someone with implements. I was known as Vladislav the Poker.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav continues his confessional about his torturing past.
jokes.punchline: His fearsome historical epithet — 'Vladislav the Poker' — is a deliberately anticlimactic name for a feared medieval torturer. (Also a sly reference to Vlad the Impaler.)
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. 'Vladislav the Poker' is perfect: it's funny as a name (anticlimactic vs. 'Vlad the Impaler'), it's funny as a description of medieval torture reduced to 'poking with implements,' and it has a double meaning (poker as in one who pokes, but also the mundane household object). Economy is 9 — four words carry enormous comedic weight. The historical allusion makes it richer for those who catch it. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Confessional about Viago: 'Viago is a little... pedantic.' Then Viago at the meeting: '...and the rubbish, I did that. Deacon, on dishes and it still hasn't moved in 5 years.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav gives his opinion of Viago in confessional.
jokes.punchline: Vladislav calls him 'pedantic,' immediately cutting to Viago obsessively itemizing who did what chore, proving the point exactly.
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary cut — character describes a trait, we immediately see it in action. Functional and well-executed. The 'pedantic' label is accurate and mildly funny, with solid editing comedy.

jokes.text: Confessional: Viago was 'an 18th century dandy. So he can be very fussy. He nags and nags.'
jokes.setup: Documentary context-setting about Viago.
jokes.punchline: '18th century dandy' as an explanation for his fussiness — a character-type that maps perfectly onto his nagging flatmate behaviour.
jokes.explanation: Character-building comedy that works without being outstanding. '18th century dandy' is a good historical tag that immediately conjures a recognizable type. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: 'I'm so embarrassed when people come over here.' / 'Why does it matter? You bring them over to kill them!'
jokes.setup: Viago is mortified about the state of the flat for visitors.
jokes.punchline: Deacon's entirely logical rejoinder: the visitors are murder victims, so their comfort and opinion is irrelevant.
jokes.explanation: Second iteration of the 'why clean for murder victims' joke. Gets a solid laugh because the logic is unassailable — Viago's anxiety is genuinely silly given the context. The repetition reinforces Deacon's character as the only one with any practical sense about their situation.

jokes.text: Viago complains about blood all over his antique couch. 'Which one, the red one?' / 'Well, it's red now, yeah.'
jokes.setup: Viago frets about blood getting on his nice couch.
jokes.punchline: Vladislav asks 'which one, the red one?' implying all their furniture has been bloodstained at some point — 'well it's red now' confirming that murder has permanently redecorated.
jokes.explanation: Smart two-beat joke. 'The red one?' is funny because it implies blood-redecorating is routine; 'it's red now' confirms it with perfect economy. The domestic complaint framing makes the dark punchline land harder. Well-structured exchange.

jokes.text: Viago: 'If you're going to eat a victim on my nice clean couch, put down some newspaper on the floor and some towels. It's not hard to do.' / 'We're vampires! We don't put down towels.' / 'Some vampires do.' / 'Well, not serious ones!'
jokes.setup: Viago has house rules about blood-related mess management.
jokes.punchline: The 'serious vampires' callback: 'not serious ones!' is a reprise of the dishes argument, now applied to victim-eating etiquette. The running gag reveals this is a persistent philosophical divide.
jokes.explanation: The 'serious vampires' construction becomes a running gag here, applied to a new context (murder etiquette vs. dish-doing). The payoff is enhanced for those who caught the first instance. Character-specific to Deacon's rebellious vampire identity. The addition of towels-for-victims is an inspired escalation of the domestic-meets-murderous premise.

jokes.text: Cut to Deacon alone doing the dishes, clearly seething. 'This is bullshit.'
jokes.setup: The flat meeting ended with Deacon agreeing to do his dishes.
jokes.punchline: He's doing them, but cannot contain his resentment — 'this is bullshit' as a muttered aside while performing the most mundane of tasks, the gap between vampire ego and domestic reality complete.
jokes.explanation: Perfect punctuation to the flat-meeting sequence. 'This is bullshit' from a centuries-old vampire doing dishes is the entire joke of the film in four words. High economy score. The long pause before the line (implied by the timestamp gap) adds to the impact.

jokes.text: 'Well, I became a vampire when I was 16. That is why I always look 16. In those days, of course, life was tough for a 16 year old.'
jokes.setup: Deacon begins a confessional about his backstory.
jokes.punchline: 'That is why I always look 16' — a matter-of-fact self-description from someone presenting as a teenager talking about ancient vampire history. 'Life was tough for a 16 year old' in those days doubles the bathos.
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan self-awareness. The joke is in the gap between how Deacon looks (a teenager) and his ancient experience, presented with total equanimity. 'Life was tough for a 16 year old' is a mild escalation that lets the audience fill in the historical gap.

jokes.text: 'Vampires have had a pretty bad rec. We're not these mopey old creatures who live in castles. And while some, most of us are, a lot are... bats.'
jokes.setup: Deacon begins defending vampires against stereotypes.
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts himself ('most of us are' castle-dwellers), then trails off into 'a lot are... bats' — both a literal and figurative admission that undercuts the entire PR pitch.
jokes.explanation: Self-undermining rhetoric is a reliable comedy tool and this is a good execution. The improvised quality of the self-correction ('some, most of us are') feels authentic to the mockumentary format. The final 'a lot are... bats' is a nice double-meaning punchline.

jokes.text: 'I was a Nazi vampire.'
jokes.setup: Documentary confessional about vampires integrating into New Zealand society.
jokes.punchline: The blunt, matter-of-fact confession — 'I was a Nazi vampire' — delivered without preamble or apology, as though it's a minor biographical detail.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum impact. 'I was a Nazi vampire' is the kind of line that gets quoted forever — it compounds two already-extreme character identities and presents them with zero affect. Economy score of 10 is warranted: no word is wasted and no word could be removed. The pause before the follow-up explanation makes it even funnier.

jokes.text: 'After the war, which the Nazi's lost... I don't know, if you know that the Nazi's lost... that war. If you were a Nazi, after the war... and if you were a vampire... and if you were a Nazi vampire... No way. I was out of there.'
jokes.setup: Following 'I was a Nazi vampire,' the vampire explains his emigration rationale.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate parenthetical clarification ('I don't know if you know that the Nazis lost') plus the building triple-condition structure ('if you were a Nazi... and a vampire... and a Nazi vampire') builds to 'No way. I was out of there' — a completely reasonable conclusion delivered with a shrug.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in escalation comedy. The aside ('I don't know if you know the Nazis lost') is condescending absurdism, the triple-condition structure builds beautifully, and 'No way. I was out of there' is a perfectly anticlimactic button. The logic is impeccable: of COURSE a Nazi vampire had to leave. The understatement carries the whole thing.

jokes.text: 'After the war, which the Nazi's lost... I don't know, if you know that the Nazi's lost... that war. If you were a Nazi, after the war... and if you were a vampire... and if you were a Nazi vampire... No way. I was out of there.'
jokes.setup: He's explaining why he left after the war
jokes.punchline: The joke escalates through 'if you were a Nazi... and if you were a vampire... and if you were a NAZI vampire' — the cumulative absurdity of combining two 'in hiding' identities, capped with the most understated possible conclusion: 'No way. I was out of there.'
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is beautifully constructed — three stacked conditional 'if' clauses building to an impossible intersection of post-war hiding identities, then 'No way. I was out of there.' The parenthetical '...I don't know if you know that the Nazi's lost...that war' is a perfect aside, as if the interviewer might not know basic history. The logic holds — a vampire Nazi would be doubly hunted — making it intellectually funny as well as absurdly funny.

jokes.text: Viago's confessional: He came to New Zealand for love, describes the woman as 'absolutely amazing,' 'smitten' — his servant Phillip put the wrong postage on his coffin, journey took 18 months — she was married when he arrived.
jokes.setup: Viago narrates a romantic backstory about chasing a human woman to New Zealand.
jokes.punchline: The grand romantic gesture (following love across the world) is undermined by: (a) servant putting wrong postage on his coffin, (b) 18-month postal journey, (c) she was already married. Each beat is funnier than the last.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured micro-tragedy with escalating comedy. 'He put the wrong postage on my coffin' is a sublime line — it makes the vampire's travel logistics suddenly very mundane and very wrong. The 18-month journey by coffin-post, arriving to find her married, is Viago's character in a nutshell: romantic, ineffectual, slightly tragic. High character integration because this story is very specifically Viago.

jokes.text: Beat: Viago has clearly been pining for this lost love. He shows the camera her portrait. 'There she is. That's me, I put myself in there too.'
jokes.setup: Viago produces a cherished miniature portrait of his lost love.
jokes.punchline: 'That's me, I put myself in there too' — he painted himself into her portrait, which is both desperately romantic and completely bizarre.
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny. The clarification 'I put myself in there too' implies the portrait was originally just of her and he added himself — a haunting and pathetic act of romantic longing that works because Viago says it with complete dignity. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Viago shows a silver locket she gave him. 'She told me it was pure silver. Unfortunately... we vampires cannot wear silver.' He attempts to wear it on camera and visibly burns. '...Yeah. It's about as long as I can wear that.'
jokes.setup: Viago explains his lost love gave him a precious parting gift.
jokes.punchline: She gave a vampire a silver locket — either accidentally or not — and he has been trying to wear it. He demonstrates by burning himself, then states with pained understatement 'it's about as long as I can wear that.'
jokes.explanation: One of the most emotionally layered jokes in the reel. The silver locket is funny on its surface (what a terrible gift for a vampire), but the real comedy comes from Viago STILL TRYING TO WEAR IT — the pathetic devotion to a painful object because she gave it to him. 'It's about as long as I can wear that' as a measured, pained understatement is perfect. The physical comedy of the burning amplifies it. This is characterisation and comedy fused perfectly.

jokes.text: The vampires prepare to go out into Wellington. 'One of the unfortunate things about not having a reflection is that you don't know exactly what you look like.'
jokes.setup: The vampires are getting dressed for a night out.
jokes.punchline: The observation that not having a reflection is 'unfortunate' in a vanity context — presented as the main inconvenience of being a vampire — is a classic understatement. The setup for the visual comedy to follow.
jokes.explanation: A reliable observation on vampire mythology reframed as a fashion inconvenience. Works as setup for the subsequent scene more than as a standalone joke. Competent and consistent with the film's register.

jokes.text: Visual gag: A floating 'ghost cup' — tea/coffee held by an invisible vampire (Viago, seen only by the audience) — drifting through the air as the vampires use each other as mirrors.
jokes.setup: Viago explains they help each other with appearance since mirrors are useless.
jokes.punchline: A cup visibly floating in mid-air, which Viago cheerfully narrates as 'Look! A ghost cup! Floating all by itself!' — he is delighted by his own invisibility as a parlor trick.
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag that uses the mockumentary format cleverly — the camera catches what the vampires can't see in a mirror. Viago's delight in his own invisibility ('Look! A ghost cup!') is very on-brand. Works better visually than on paper.

jokes.text: 'We can give each other feedback and help each other out until we're looking great.' — vampires sketching each other in lieu of mirrors to help each other dress.
jokes.setup: Without reflections, the vampires need an alternative method to check their outfits.
jokes.punchline: They draw portraits of each other as a mirror substitute — the elaborate workaround for a simple problem.
jokes.explanation: Inventive practical consequence of vampirism — the portrait-as-mirror is a clever piece of world-building comedy. The image of ancient vampires earnestly sketching each other to help with outfit choices is visually very funny.

jokes.text: The vampires help each other get dressed since they can't see themselves in mirrors. 'Yes, some of our clothes are from victims. We might bite someone and then... you think, ooh, those are some nice pants!'
jokes.setup: The vampires are discussing their wardrobe while dressing for the night.
jokes.punchline: Victim-clothing-as-fashion-haul: murder as a secondary source of nice trousers, delivered with the enthusiasm of someone describing a good charity shop find.
jokes.explanation: A dark comedy gem in miniature. The specificity of 'ooh, those are some nice pants!' after a murder is exactly the kind of bathetic detail that characterizes the film. The shopping-trip register applied to post-kill scavenging is well-judged.

jokes.text: 'Yes, some of our clothes are from victims. We might bite someone and then... you think, ooh, those are some nice pants!'
jokes.setup: Discussion of their wardrobe and fashion choices.
jokes.punchline: Their clothes come from murder victims — specifically, biting someone and then admiring their pants. The consumerist aside ('ooh, those are some nice pants!') in the context of murder is perfectly grotesque.
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy joke — the victim-as-wardrobe-source is a great absurd detail, and 'ooh, those are some nice pants!' captures the mundane consumerism of a vampire admiring their kill's outfit. The casualness of it is perfectly calibrated.

jokes.text: Viago describes his style as 'Dead But Delicious.' 'We are the bait. But we're also the trap. Hello, ladies.'
jokes.setup: Viago explains vampire fashion philosophy.
jokes.punchline: 'Dead But Delicious' as a self-coined style descriptor, then practicing his seductive opener ('Hello, ladies') in the mirror-free dressing room.
jokes.explanation: 'Dead But Delicious' is a quotable, specific piece of character-flavored language. The 'bait and trap' formulation is structurally neat. 'Hello, ladies' as a practice seduction is a good button that shows Viago's sincere but slightly tragic romantic ambitions.

jokes.text: The vampires sweep out of the house dramatically. 'And my love, we are ready to go into town and party! Vampire... vampire style.'
jokes.setup: The vampires have finished getting ready.
jokes.punchline: 'Vampire... vampire style' — the slight pause and repetition suggests Viago thought he was going to say something cooler and then just said the most literal thing possible.
jokes.explanation: Mild comedy from the anticlimax of 'vampire style' — built up to but then deflated by its own literalness. Characteristic of Viago's endearing earnestness. Not a strong joke in isolation but serves the sequence well.

jokes.text: Walking in Wellington: Viago narrates feeling like they're fitting in for one brief moment — cut to someone shouting 'Homos!' from offscreen.
jokes.setup: Viago lovingly describes the sensation of blending in with modern Wellington nightlife.
jokes.punchline: His reverie is broken by a stranger's homophobic slur — implying that the vampires' elaborate historical dress makes them look gay to locals, not vampiric, and that Wellington streets are not exactly welcoming.
jokes.explanation: A sharp editing joke — the interruption undercuts Viago's romanticism efficiently. The implication (elaborate vampire period-dress reads as flamboyantly gay to Wellington locals) is funnier than the slur itself. Some may find the content of the slur off-putting, but in context it's directed at the punchline of the vampires failing to blend in. Economy is high.

jokes.text: The vampires try to enter a bar. 'We would like to come into the bar, please. Invite us into the bar, please.' 'Keep walking.' 'You invite us in!'
jokes.setup: Vampires need to be invited in — an ancient supernatural rule — applied to a modern nightclub door policy.
jokes.punchline: The vampires earnestly asking to be formally invited in by the bouncer — 'We would like to come into the bar, please' as a supernatural necessity that sounds like a very polite request from unusual patrons.
jokes.explanation: A reliable fish-out-of-water joke that works because the vampire rule (must be invited in) collides perfectly with the mundane modern context (nightclub entry). The repeated polite requests and the bouncer's dismissal is a solid three-beat comedic exchange.

jokes.text: 'Obvious vampire.' / 'Joline! Hello! How embarrassing.' / 'He's a guy I used to work with when I was human.' / 'Is he gone?' / 'Yeah, he's gone.' / 'I've been draining him all night.'
jokes.setup: While outside, they encounter another vampire — a woman who appears to know one of the group.
jokes.punchline: The vampires note the new arrival is an 'obvious vampire,' she cheerfully reconnects with an old work acquaintance, then immediately reveals she's been draining him all night — casual murder as social small talk.
jokes.explanation: Good miniature dark comedy. 'Is he gone?' followed by 'I've been draining him all night / Been a very thirsty girl' reframes the encounter with the old colleague as predatory from the start. The cheerful female vampire's affect sells it.

jokes.text: Child vampire: 'What are you doing tonight? Going to kill some perverts?' 'Yeah, we're meeting a pedophile.' 'Cool.'
jokes.setup: Documentary note: 'Being bitten as a little boy or little girl you always go to look the same age.' We see a child-vampire making small talk.
jokes.punchline: The child vampire asks in a completely normal kid-making-plans voice whether they're 'going to kill some perverts,' and the casual confirmation ('yeah, we're meeting a pedophile / Cool') treats targeted murder as a wholesome evening activity.
jokes.explanation: Superb dark comedy. The concept of a child vampire casually asking if they're 'going to kill some perverts' is unexpected and funny; the matter-of-fact confirmation and equally casual 'Cool' makes it a complete, perfectly-paced exchange. It also implies vampire vigilante justice which adds an extra layer of absurdity. Very good economy.

jokes.text: 'The Big Kumara is vampire owned and operated, so we could always get in. It's the hottest night spot for vampires in Wellington.'
jokes.setup: The vampires couldn't get into the regular bar.
jokes.punchline: Wellington has a vampire-owned nightclub — 'the hottest night spot for vampires in Wellington' — delivered as though this is an ordinary piece of local knowledge.
jokes.explanation: Solid worldbuilding comedy. The idea of a vampire-exclusive Wellington nightclub called 'The Big Kumara' is funny in its specificity and mundanity. 'The hottest night spot for vampires in Wellington' implies there's a ranking of such establishments. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Inside the club, negotiating what kind of victims Deacon's familiar should bring: 'Perhaps some virgins?' / 'Any kind of preference in terms of gender?' / 'Maybe some ladies? Perhaps a guy? One of each?' / 'One of each should be cool.'
jokes.setup: The vampires are placing a 'victim order' via their human familiar.
jokes.punchline: The negotiations are conducted with the register of ordering a takeaway or making restaurant reservations — gender preference, quantity, one of each — applied to selecting murder victims.
jokes.explanation: Classic WWDITS register — murder logistics handled with the casual specificity of a food order. 'One of each should be cool' is a good button. Works through accumulated deadpan rather than a single sharp joke.

jokes.text: Deacon asking his familiar Nick for virgins: 'Perhaps some virgins? Any kind of preference in terms of gender or? Maybe some ladies? Perhaps a guy? One of each? One of each should be cool.'
jokes.setup: Deacon is sending his human familiar Nick on a recruitment mission to find victims.
jokes.punchline: The request for victims is handled with the awkward hedging of someone ordering food — trying to seem non-judgmental about gender, eventually settling on 'one of each' as a reasonable compromise, all while ordering people to their deaths.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy — the conscientious hedging ('any preference in terms of gender?') applied to ordering murder victims. The 'one of each' resolution implies Deacon is trying to be inclusive even in his predation. Well-observed awkward exchange.

jokes.text: Confessional from Jackie: 'My relationship with Deacon is... well, I'm his familiar. He's my Master. He tells me what to do, I do it. We have the kind of master-servant relationship which works nicely. Actually.'
jokes.setup: Documentary interview with Deacon's human familiar about their relationship dynamic.
jokes.punchline: 'Which works nicely. Actually.' — the 'Actually' is a tiny hesitation that implies it doesn't really work nicely, that this is a rationalisation, delivered as a documentary subject who's not fully convincing herself.
jokes.explanation: Good performance-based joke. 'Actually' at the end of a positive statement is a mockumentary staple used here with real precision. Jackie's self-deception is communicated entirely through that one-word qualifier. Character-specific.

jokes.text: Blood explanation at the nightclub: 'It's a little bit of blood. Um, my husband, he's a, he's a hemophiliac. You know, someone who bleeds a lot.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav has blood on him and is apparently explaining it to someone at the club.
jokes.punchline: He invents a 'hemophiliac husband' cover story, then helpfully defines hemophiliac ('you know, someone who bleeds a lot') as though the person might not know the word — an absurd combination of deception and condescension.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the flimsy cover story is funny, but the parenthetical definition of hemophiliac is even funnier because it implies Vladislav thinks he needs to educate the person he's lying to. Character-specific to Vladislav's slightly superior air.

jokes.text: Jackie negotiates victim age range. 'Any kind of age range?' / 'Young.' / 'But not, not kids?' / 'Not kids. 18 to 30.' / 'Definitely younger than yourself.' / 'Okay, so 18 to 30.'
jokes.setup: Continuing the victim-ordering scene.
jokes.punchline: 'Definitely younger than yourself' — a casually devastating age insult directed at Jackie (the familiar) in the middle of a murder logistics discussion, delivered as a practical specification.
jokes.explanation: Good miniature insult embedded in the procedural victim-selection dialogue. The age comment is cruel but matter-of-fact — nobody acknowledges it as an insult, it's just a data point, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: The 'dinner party' framing: 'So it's a dinner party?' / 'I'll be there? Yes!' / 'The guys will be there?' / 'Yes, we will all be there. We will dress up. And then... eat them.' / 'Should be fun.' / 'Okay, great.'
jokes.setup: Jackie is clarifying logistics of the victim-luring plan.
jokes.punchline: 'We will all be there. We will dress up. And then... eat them. Should be fun.' — a dinner party rsvp with murder confirmed as the evening's main activity, delivered with genuine social enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: The 'we will dress up. And then... eat them' beats are perfectly timed — the pause before 'eat them' and the immediate 'should be fun' treat murder as a dinner party activity. The structure mirrors actual dinner party planning which makes the dark pivot land harder.

jokes.text: Jackie tries to bring up 'the deal' (eternal life) during the victim-ordering conversation. Gets brushed aside: 'You don't know of a night dentist? Because I have this thing here.' / 'I was just wondering if we could talk about the deal.' / 'Hm? The dishes?'
jokes.setup: Jackie wants to discuss the promised deal with Deacon (eternal life for services rendered).
jokes.punchline: She keeps getting interrupted — first by the dentist question, then by Deacon misunderstanding 'the deal' as being about dishes. The more she tries to raise it, the more she's dismissed.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy — Jackie's desperation to discuss the eternal-life deal is systemically ignored. 'The dishes?' as Deacon's first association with 'the deal' is a nice callback that also shows how little he cares about his end of the bargain.

jokes.text: Jackie's confessional about the deal: 'The deal is that he is going to give me eternal life. Um, which is... very exciting. Well, I just feel like I kind of reached my potential and I wouldn't want to kind of, get any older before I kind of... I just feel like I'm the best version of myself that I can be.'
jokes.setup: Jackie explains why she's doing Deacon's bidding.
jokes.punchline: The life-coach/self-help language applied to 'I want to stop aging before I get uglier' — 'I'm the best version of myself that I can be' as a reason to become an immortal creature of the night.
jokes.explanation: Modern self-help vernacular ('best version of myself') applied to vampire servitude and vanity is sharp social observation. Jackie's character is established here as someone who has thoroughly rationalized her situation. The hedged, meandering delivery adds to the cringe.

jokes.text: Jackie lists her services: 'doing your plans and... doing your dry-cleaning. Now I'm doing your dishes.' / Deacon's non-response. / 'And the dentist and it's just taking an awful long time.'
jokes.setup: Jackie itemizes 4.5 years of service hoping to shame Deacon into action.
jokes.punchline: The list descends from 'your plans' (possibly sinister vampire schemes) to 'dry-cleaning' to 'dishes' to apparently making dental appointments — the mundanity of servitude escalating downward rather than up.
jokes.explanation: The descending list of services is a good bit of character-revealing escalation. 'Doing the dishes' landing in a list of a vampire's familiar's duties is a callback to the flat-meeting, connecting two threads. The dentist appointment is a good final detail.

jokes.text: 'Be gone!' / 'Okay. I see you later!' / 'Okay.'
jokes.setup: Jackie has been pressing for the eternal life deal.
jokes.punchline: Deacon dismisses her with the theatrical vampire command 'Be gone!' — she immediately complies cheerfully ('I see you later!') as though it's a normal goodbye.
jokes.explanation: 'Be gone!' is a perfect character moment for Deacon — reverting to theatrical vampire register when cornered. Jackie's breezy 'I see you later!' shows her complete normalization of the supernatural master-servant dynamic. Good economy.

jokes.text: Viago's confessional on victim hospitality: 'I like to make a real evening of it. Play some music. Maybe give them some nice wine. It's their last moment alive so why not make it a nice experience.'
jokes.setup: Viago explains his philosophy on feeding.
jokes.punchline: He treats murder victims like dinner guests — music, wine, nice experience — because that's who Viago is: a considerate host even when killing you.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration — this is the definitive Viago moment. His compulsive hospitality extended to murder victims ('it's their last moment alive so why not make it a nice experience') is simultaneously funny and oddly moving. It could ONLY come from this character, perfectly expressing the tension between his genuine kindness and his necessary violence.

jokes.text: Viago's murder date sequence: He's charming a woman over wine, she's talking about going back to uni and traveling to Spain and Italy — he nods along politely, clearly about to kill her, occasionally interrupting to arrange newspapers on the floor.
jokes.setup: Viago is following his stated philosophy of making the victim's last moments nice.
jokes.punchline: The parallel tracking of her future plans (uni, travel, Spain, Italy) against Viago quietly preparing to murder her — the irony of listening attentively to dreams she'll never fulfill while positioning newspaper.
jokes.explanation: Excellent sustained cringe comedy. The woman discussing her travel plans — a very ordinary, relatable young-person monologue — is devastating in context. Viago placing newspaper while she talks about Italy is perfect dark comedy. The callback to both the hospitality speech and the flat-meeting newspaper/towels argument adds a layer for attentive viewers.

jokes.text: Viago attempting to be a gracious host to a victim, chatting about her going back to Uni and traveling to Spain, Italy, and London — before killing her.
jokes.setup: Viago is playing nice host, putting the woman at ease with small talk about her future plans.
jokes.punchline: The irony of her excitedly describing future travel plans (Spain, Italy, London) that she will never take because Viago is about to kill her — Viago nodding along encouragingly.
jokes.explanation: Dark sustained irony — the victim's future plans (Uni, travel) are enthusiastically discussed with the host who is about to end them. Viago's sincere interest ('Yeah!') is what makes it funny rather than grim. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'Shit!' — Viago's immediate exclamation off-camera, implying catastrophic blood mess.
jokes.setup: We know from Viago's earlier concern about mess that this murder is going badly.
jokes.punchline: The single panicked 'Shit!' from offscreen, implying the blood management has gone completely wrong despite all preparations.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word, perfectly placed. 'Shit!' from someone who fussed about mess is the ideal payoff. The offscreen audio-only format makes it funnier because we don't see it, our imagination fills it in. Strong callback payoff.

jokes.text: 'Well, that didn't go so great. Um, I hit the main artery. So, yeah, it's a real mess in there, um... On the upside, I think she had a really good time.'
jokes.setup: Viago reports back to the camera after the disastrous feeding.
jokes.punchline: 'On the upside, I think she had a really good time.' — his primary concern, even in the wake of a catastrophically messy murder, is whether the victim enjoyed herself. The hospitality instinct survives everything.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel and possibly the film. 'On the upside, I think she had a really good time' is a stunning punchline — it's the culmination of everything we know about Viago (his hospitality instinct, his fussiness about mess, his genuine consideration) expressed in a single sentence about an accidental arterial murder. The 'on the upside' construction, applied to a messy killing, is precisely calibrated. Character integration is 9.5 — this is the essential Viago line. Comparable in quality to the vasectomy anchor at the top of the scale.

jokes.text: Vladislav narrates finding a late-night television viewer as a potential victim. 'I'm just going to use hypnosis on her... See me...' Long pause. 'She can't, she can't see me from that angle.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav sets up hypnosis on a TV-watching woman, confident in his ancient powers.
jokes.punchline: 'She can't, she can't see me from that angle.' — the master hypnotist is foiled not by supernatural countermeasures but by his own positioning. He stepped into her blind spot.
jokes.explanation: Good comedy of incompetence. The bathos of an ancient powerful hypnotist being foiled by geometry is perfectly in keeping with the film's thesis about vampires as bumbling flatlanders. The repeated 'See me...' with the long pause before the mundane explanation is well-timed.

jokes.text: Confessional about Vladislav: 'Vladislav used to be extremely powerful. He could hypnotize crowds of people. Great orgies. 20-30 women. He could turn into all sorts of animals. But now he never get the faces right. He would kill anybody. Men, women. Children. Burning... everything. It was totally great. But he suffered a humiliating defeat... at the hands of his arch nemesis... The Beast.'
jokes.setup: Viago provides documentary context for Vladislav's current diminished state.
jokes.punchline: Multiple punchlines in sequence: 'Great orgies. 20-30 women.' (casual power flex), 'now he never gets the faces right' (specific, absurd diminishment), 'It was totally great' (re: mass murder of children), and the melodramatic 'The Beast' as arch nemesis — all delivered in the same flat confessional tone.
jokes.explanation: A dense joke sequence delivered as a single confessional. 'It was totally great' about mass murdering children is audacious dark comedy; 'he never gets the faces right' when turning into animals is a brilliantly specific detail suggesting his power has degraded in a weird way. 'The Beast' as a dramatic, unexplained nemesis is excellent misdirection setup for later payoff. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: 'But he suffered a humiliating defeat... at the hands of his arch nemesis... The Beast.'
jokes.setup: Documentary narration explains why Vladislav is no longer at his former peak.
jokes.punchline: 'The Beast' — delivered as a capital-B title of terrible power and mystery. The 'The' is doing enormous work: whatever The Beast is, it sounds maximally frightening.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for what will presumably be a later payoff — 'The Beast' as an ominous title is played completely straight. Functions as a tease/mystery rather than a complete joke in itself, but the gravity of the reveal is funny in context of Vladislav's current inability to hypnotize one television-watching woman.

jokes.text: Vladislav tries hypnosis again from a new position: 'See me...' Cut to: she opens the door and says 'Would you like to come inside?' — the hypnosis appears to have worked.
jokes.setup: After failing due to wrong angle, Vladislav repositions and tries again.
jokes.punchline: It works — but the callback to the 'must be invited in' rule means being invited in is both the vampire's supernatural requirement AND the hypnosis payoff, neatly tying together two jokes.
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke — the 'would you like to come inside?' invitation is simultaneously the hypnosis working and the vampire-rule payoff. It's a callback that doubles the comedic value of both the bar-entry scene and the failed hypnosis. Well-structured reel-closing beat.

jokes.text: 'And, he's never been the same.' / 'See me...' — Vladislav resuming his failed hypnosis attempt after the full context of his former greatness has been established.
jokes.setup: We've just been told Vladislav used to hypnotize crowds, kill armies, and was defeated only by The Beast.
jokes.punchline: Cut back to him standing outside a window in a Wellington suburb, still trying to hypnotize one woman watching TV: 'See me...' The gap between his legendary past and his present incompetence is now maximally apparent.
jokes.explanation: Superb structural joke. The insert of Viago's testimony about Vladislav's former greatness (crowds, orgies, armies, burning everything) sandwiched between two identical 'See me...' attempts creates perfect comedic architecture. The second 'See me...' lands infinitely harder than the first because we now know what he's fallen from. This is editing-as-comedy at its best. The 'See me' repetition is both callback and punchline.

jokes.text: Deacon explains they need 'victims' while warmly welcoming guests
jokes.setup: Jackie introduces her guests as if this is a normal social visit; Deacon's narration framing them as victims is delivered as a mundane logistical statement
jokes.punchline: The word 'victims' is slipped in with zero menace, treating murder as routine hospitality planning
jokes.explanation: Classic WWDITS deadpan — the horror framing (murder) colliding with mundane hospitality language is the show's core comedic engine. Well executed, though it's a standard register for the film.

jokes.text: Deacon explains he can't be envious of or like the victims — because then they become victims
jokes.setup: Deacon is trying to explain the etiquette of selecting dinner guests
jokes.punchline: His circular, almost bureaucratic logic about victim selection — you can't like them or they become off-limits as victims — reveals a weirdly principled monster
jokes.explanation: The improvised, stumbling delivery makes this feel authentic but slightly loose. The concept is funny — a vampire with victim-selection ethics — but the execution is a bit muddled.

jokes.text: Josefine insists she sat next to the vampire in English class and he used to call her 'the Jacksersist'; both characters argue over who started the nickname
jokes.setup: Deacon (a centuries-old vampire) is trying to lure Josefine as a victim; she cheerfully reminds him they were classmates
jokes.punchline: Instead of seduction or menace, the encounter devolves into a petty argument about who invented a school nickname, completely undercutting any vampire mystique
jokes.explanation: Strongly character-integrated: an ancient vampire reduced to a schoolyard squabble. The bathos of 'you started it / no you started it' from a predator who was about to murder someone is excellent comedic deflation. The improv energy makes it feel genuinely awkward and real.

jokes.text: "She's in." — Deacon's terse camera-to-camera aside after the nickname argument concludes
jokes.setup: The whole awkward reunion/nickname argument seemed to derail any predatory intent
jokes.punchline: Deacon calmly confirms she's been selected as a victim anyway — the social awkwardness was apparently just part of the process
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words that recontextualize everything. The deadpan pivot from awkward social exchange to cold predator logic in a single breath is classic WWDITS. High quotability for its blunt brevity.

jokes.text: "Nick, are you a virgin at all?" — vampire asking a dinner guest point-blank about his virginity status
jokes.setup: Nick has been brought to the house; the vampires need to assess the dinner guests
jokes.punchline: The blunt, socially inappropriate question about virginity — asked with the clinical curiosity of someone checking ingredient quality — is completely wrong in every social register
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup. The phrasing 'at all' is a lovely awkward qualifier that makes it feel even more socially clumsy. The confusion over virgin blood as quality-control rather than symbolic is well-played.

jokes.text: "I think we drink virgin blood because... it sounds cool."
jokes.setup: The vampires debate the vampire mythology of virgin blood with apparent seriousness
jokes.punchline: The centuries-old tradition is deflated to pure aesthetics — they do it because it sounds cool, with no deeper reason
jokes.explanation: Genuinely sharp. It deconstructs vampire mythology by suggesting the mystique is entirely performative — they don't actually know why, it just sounds better. The honesty of the admission is funnier than any elaborate mythology explanation would be. High economy.

jokes.text: "If you're going to eat a sandwich, you will just enjoy it more if you knew no one had fucked it."
jokes.setup: Deacon is trying to explain the appeal of virgin blood using an everyday analogy
jokes.punchline: The sandwich analogy is both logical in its own weird way and completely, grotesquely wrong as a comparison — the juxtaposition of the mundane (sandwich) and the obscene makes it land hard
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the film. It earns 9+ on every dimension: the concept is completely original, the structure is a perfect analogy-with-subverted-conclusion, it could ONLY come from a vampire trying to explain his world in human terms, the economy is immaculate (one sentence), and it earns the laugh through pure unexpected logic rather than any shortcut. 'No one had fucked it' is the exact wrong word, delivered with absolute conviction. Genuinely memorable, comparable in quotability and craft to the film's most famous lines.

jokes.text: "Who would have sex with her? I wouldn't." / "I would." — vampires debate Josefine's virginity/attractiveness
jokes.setup: The vampires are trying to identify which guest is a virgin by assessing their social desirability
jokes.punchline: One vampire's dismissive cruelty is immediately countered by another's sincere disagreement — the antisocial logic of the debate makes both responses equally appalling
jokes.explanation: The comedic mechanism (clinical dehumanization through sexual desirability rating) works in context, but it leans on shock cruelty rather than wit. The two-beat structure (dismissal + sincere correction) saves it somewhat.

jokes.text: "Do you like bisghetti?" — vampire offers pasta to dinner guests
jokes.setup: The vampire is pivoting from the awkward virgin discussion to hosting duties
jokes.punchline: The vampire pronounces 'spaghetti' as 'bisghetti' — a childlike mispronunciation from an ancient creature, suggesting centuries of language drift or willful eccentricity
jokes.explanation: "Bisghetti" becomes a running gag through the reel — the initial plant here is the comedic foundation. The mispronunciation from a creature who's supposedly lived centuries is delightfully absurd. High quotability and rewatch value as the setup for what follows.

jokes.text: The staged bisghetti reveal — vampire explains his 'favorite trick' of presenting worms as spaghetti in a talking-head confessional
jokes.setup: Deacon explains to camera that he has a "favorite trick" — presenting guests with bisghetti
jokes.punchline: The elaborate theater of presenting worms as pasta, explained with genuine pride as his signature move, undercuts any vampire menace with the enthusiasm of a mediocre party host
jokes.explanation: The earnest pride in what is objectively a low-tier prank is well-integrated into Deacon's character. It humanizes him in a ridiculous way — a vampire with a 'signature trick' at dinner parties.

jokes.text: "Please, Nick. Eat some bisghetti." — solemn, formal invitation to eat worms
jokes.setup: The trick has been explained; now the execution — the gravity with which the invitation is delivered
jokes.punchline: The formal solemnity of "Please, Nick" applied to eating a plate of worms is perfect deadpan — treating it like an elaborate ritual rather than a juvenile prank
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of a sincere invitation to eat worms, using the vampire's established mispronunciation, earns the callback tag. The formality is the joke.

jokes.text: "I didn't realize you enjoy eating worms, Nick."
jokes.setup: Nick has just discovered the bisghetti are worms and is reacting with horror
jokes.punchline: Deacon calmly observes Nick's disgust as if it reveals a quirky personal preference, flipping victim and trickster
jokes.explanation: The reframing of Nick's horror as a revealed personal food preference is a clean bit of deadpan misdirection. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: "We stole that idea from The Lost Boys. But I put a nice twist on it."
jokes.setup: The worm-bisghetti prank has just been executed; Deacon is explaining the inspiration
jokes.punchline: A vampire casually admits to plagiarizing a trick from a vampire movie and is proud of his 'twist' — a moment of meta self-awareness that punctures vampire mythology while also being endearingly competitive
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent meta joke. A real vampire admitting he got his tricks from a vampire movie — and is proud that he improved on them — is conceptually sharp, perfectly character-integrated (Deacon is vain and competitive), and delivered with beautiful economy. The 'nice twist' pride is the killer detail. Approaches 8-level quality: original, structurally crisp, could only come from this character, earns the laugh through wit not shortcut.

jokes.text: "Nick. How does it feel to have a snake for a penis?"
jokes.setup: The worm-bisghetti trick has just played out; there's apparently a secondary hex or illusion affecting Nick
jokes.punchline: The completely unexpected question — delivered with the same clinical calm as the virgin inquiry — reveals a second, far more disturbing prank that wasn't telegraphed at all
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best individual lines. The structure is perfect misdirection — we're absorbed in the worm prank, then a completely new horror is introduced with zero warning, delivered as a polite inquiry. The economy is flawless: nine words that cause complete comedic whiplash. The phrasing 'how does it feel' (as if taking a survey) is what elevates it beyond a simple shock joke.

jokes.text: "My penis has disappeared. It's a cobra snake." / "Nobody is gonna mistake your penis for a cobra, Nick, okay?"
jokes.setup: Nick is panicking about his apparently snake-transformed penis; Jackie responds
jokes.punchline: Jackie's pragmatic reassurance — nobody would mistake it for a COBRA specifically — implies the penis might be small enough that a large snake is out of the question, but also that she has firsthand knowledge
jokes.explanation: The layered joke here is excellent: Jackie's specific objection to 'cobra' (why not a smaller snake?) and the implied insider knowledge both land simultaneously. The escalation from worms to snake-penis maintains the comedic momentum without feeling forced.

jokes.text: Nick's post-escape talking head: "Look, these freaks spike my bisghetti, make my cock turn into a snake is not cool. Not cool."
jokes.setup: Nick has escaped; he's now addressing the documentary crew
jokes.punchline: His outrage is completely legitimate but his continuing use of 'bisghetti' — the vampire's mispronunciation — in his complaint is the detail that makes it. He's adopted the word without realizing it.
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'bisghetti' in his rage speech is a lovely unnoticed detail that rewards attentive viewers. His entirely reasonable outrage about the snake-cock paired with the absorbed mispronunciation shows the improv team's attention to character contamination.

jokes.text: Nick's girlfriend looks at the camera in disbelief while Nick rants — implied documentary reaction shot
jokes.setup: Nick is ranting about snake-penises and bisghetti to the documentary crew
jokes.punchline: The implied camera-stare from the girlfriend — "you don't think this is weird?" — is the straight-man reaction that grounds the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Standard mockumentary reaction beat. Functional but not distinguished. The line 'You don't think this is weird?' is a mild verbal anchor for what's presumably a visual gag.

jokes.text: "Ah no... Petyr got him. Poor guy... Who let Petyr out?"
jokes.setup: Nick has been missing; we hear sounds offscreen suggesting something terrible happened
jokes.punchline: The reaction to discovering Petyr has killed/turned Nick is not horror but mild exasperation — 'who let Petyr out?' as if he's an escaped dog who got the neighbor's mail
jokes.explanation: Superb. The bathos is perfectly constructed: someone has just been turned into a vampire (a momentous, life-ending horror), and the reaction is weary domestic complaint — 'who let the dog out?' energy applied to an ancient, terrifying creature. Character-specific (these vampires are hilariously irresponsible flatmates), economical, and genuinely quotable. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: Nick arrives at the house flying in through the window, two months later, announcing he's a vampire
jokes.setup: We cut to two months later; Nick appears at the house
jokes.punchline: He announces himself at the window — 'Hey guys!' — apparently flying in rather than using the door, as if this is a perfectly normal entrance, while the vampires react with mild annoyance
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag — Nick has become what he was fleeing from and is enthusiastically leaning into it. The window entry as casual arrival is a nice absurdist touch. Stronger as a visual moment than transcript text.

jokes.text: "Probably, I reckon best thing about being a vampire is flying. Like I've always wanted to, I think everyone has always wanted to fly. And now I can do it."
jokes.setup: Nick is doing a confessional about his new vampire life
jokes.punchline: His framing of vampirism through the most relatable childhood fantasy (flying!) — ignoring the murder, blood-drinking, and death aspects — is perfectly Nick: shallow, enthusiastic, oblivious
jokes.explanation: Very character-specific for Nick — his enthusiasm for the cool perks of vampirism while ignoring the existential horror is a good character note. The 'I think everyone has always wanted to fly' is a solid observational beat.

jokes.text: Nick apparently crashes or stumbles during his flying demonstration — implied by the 'Oh...' reaction beat
jokes.setup: Nick has just finished talking about how great flying is
jokes.punchline: He immediately demonstrates either poor form or crashes, punctuating his enthusiasm with physical failure
jokes.explanation: Classic setup-reversal: bragging about a skill followed immediately by failure. Rewatch value as it's presumably a good visual gag. Transcript-limited scoring.

jokes.text: "Nick, why don't you use the front door?" / "Why would I? I'm flying."
jokes.setup: Nick has been flying into the house through the window; a vampire housemate points out the front door exists
jokes.punchline: Nick's "Why would I? I'm flying" — delivered with the smug certainty of someone who has found a loophole in social norms — is perfect new-convert energy
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Nick as the annoying newly-turned vampire who won't stop showing off his powers is established perfectly in one exchange. 'Why would I? I'm flying.' has the cadence of a teenager who just got his driver's license and insists on driving everywhere. Character-specific, economical, and highly quotable.

jokes.text: "It was quite similar to having the flu. Except, the only difference would probably be... that my eyes bleed heaps."
jokes.setup: Nick has been systematically downplaying vampire transformation symptoms (hangover, flu)
jokes.punchline: The 'only difference' caveat — after establishing it was just like flu — is that his eyes bled profusely. The escalation of the exception makes the original minimization absurd.
jokes.explanation: Very well structured. The 'only difference' framing sets up the punchline perfectly — it promises a minor qualifier and delivers a significant physical horror. 'Heaps' (NZ slang for 'a lot') makes it even funnier as casual understatement. Good economy.

jokes.text: "The neighbors can see you flying around the house. You want to draw attention to this house, hm? You got a whole documentary crew following you around."
jokes.setup: Nick is flying around the house; a vampire is scolding him for drawing attention
jokes.punchline: He cites the documentary crew as proof that Nick is being careless about secrecy — completely oblivious to the fact that the documentary crew is a far greater privacy violation than Nick flying
jokes.explanation: Smart meta joke about the documentary format — the vampires' selective logic about what constitutes 'drawing attention' while literally being filmed is a good piece of format-awareness. The irony is clean and character-specific.

jokes.text: "I am doing an erotic dance for my friends. And you ruined it. I was in the zone."
jokes.setup: Vladislav is scolding Nick for flying; Deacon apparently has also been doing something outside
jokes.punchline: Deacon reveals he was mid-erotic-dance for the vampire friends when interrupted — delivered with absolute wounded dignity
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. 'I was in the zone' about an erotic dance performed for vampire flatmates is a perfect Deacon line — vain, dramatic, completely committed. The injured dignity elevates what could be a cheap absurdist gag.

jokes.text: "My friends are loving it." / "I love it. I saw the end of it. It looked great."
jokes.setup: Deacon insists his erotic dance was going well
jokes.punchline: Vladislav sincerely vouches for the quality of the erotic dance he witnessed — validating Deacon's artistic grievance with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: The peer validation of a vampire erotic dance, delivered with the gravity of an art critic, extends the joke well. 'I saw the end of it. It looked great.' is a lovely specific detail — implying he only caught a portion but that portion was impressive.

jokes.text: Nick's confessional about not knowing if he's accepted by the vampires: "I don't know the oldest stuff, but they're quite naive when it comes to the real world. So... I don't know, it would be cool to just hang out with them. They could teach me some stuff. But I could probably teach them a few things."
jokes.setup: Nick is processing his new vampire family situation
jokes.punchline: His framing of centuries-old vampire lords as 'quite naive' and his confidence that he could teach THEM things — while they just turned him into a vampire two months ago — is perfectly delusional
jokes.explanation: Good character note — Nick's inflated self-assessment versus his actual position (new, not accepted, recently victimized) is consistent character comedy. 'They could teach me some stuff. But I could probably teach them a few things' is the perfect phrasing of his oblivious arrogance.

jokes.text: "At the start it was like, 'Oh no, like I'm... I'm dead.' It kind of affected my friendship with normal people, my family and stuff."
jokes.setup: Nick is reflecting on his transformation into a vampire
jokes.punchline: He describes being dead as something that 'kind of affected' his social life — massive understatement
jokes.explanation: Competent understatement joke. 'Kind of affected my friendship with normal people' for being literally dead is in keeping with Nick's voice but not especially surprising at this point.

jokes.text: "They accept me for who I am. They don't even seem to know who they are. Even though... one of them killed me."
jokes.setup: Nick is warmly describing his new vampire family and how they accept him
jokes.punchline: The afterthought — 'even though one of them killed me' — arrives as a mild qualifier that he's apparently decided not to let bother him too much
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the reel. The structure is immaculate: warm, relatable sentiment (they accept me for who I am) + slight confusion (they don't know who they are) + devastating afterthought (one of them killed me). The buried 'even though' is doing enormous work. The casualness with which Nick has decided to move past his own murder as a minor relational grievance is brilliantly observed character comedy. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: Nick introducing Stu: explaining Stu works in computers, used to date his sister, and then "he can't hear me" — said in front of Stu who absolutely can hear
jokes.setup: Nick is introducing Stu to the vampires; he gives background on Stu's personal history
jokes.punchline: He segues into the sister-breakup information and then says 'he can't hear me' — Stu is standing right there and clearly can
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — Nick is simultaneously insulting/exposing Stu while believing he has plausible deniability. Functional but not especially distinctive.

jokes.text: "Just like... it really, really sucks... that I can't eat him."
jokes.setup: Nick has been warmly describing Stu as his best friend
jokes.punchline: The pivot to 'it sucks I can't eat him' — delivered with genuine regret, like a vegan at a barbecue — frames friendship and appetite as competing but equal desires
jokes.explanation: Very well-integrated character joke. The 'it really, really sucks' phrasing — with extra emphasis — mirrors the genuine frustration of someone trying to maintain a friendship while battling predatory instinct. The normalization of the desire to eat your friend is both dark and funny.

jokes.text: "I just want to like... Look at it. He's the reddest guy I know."
jokes.setup: Nick is lamenting he can't eat Stu
jokes.punchline: His specific attraction to Stu is that he's 'the reddest guy I know' — a vampire's aesthetic appreciation of a friend's blood-suggestive complexion as an attractiveness criterion
jokes.explanation: Specific and original — 'the reddest guy I know' as a vampire compliment is a lovely detail. It suggests the vampires assess humans through a completely alien aesthetic lens. The specificity ('reddest') elevates it above generic vampire humor.

jokes.text: "Right, you can hear me." — Nick, remembering Stu can hear, mid-compliment about eating him
jokes.setup: Nick has been speaking about wanting to eat Stu in front of Stu
jokes.punchline: He suddenly remembers Stu can hear — the callback to 'he can't hear me' from before — but only after already expressing his desire to consume him
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the earlier 'he can't hear me' gag — Nick's pattern of forgetting Stu is present is consistent. The horror of realizing you've just explained your desire to eat someone, TO that person, is well-played.

jokes.text: "I don't think Nick should have been turned into a vampire. He's such a dick."
jokes.setup: Nick is enthusiastically rallying everyone for a night out
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's flat-affect confessional delivering the most direct character assessment — framing an accidental vampire-turning as a social error rather than a tragedy
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. The bluntness of 'He's such a dick' as the conclusion to a centuries-old vampire's character assessment is beautifully flat. The implication that Petyr made a lifestyle error (poor victim selection) is funnier than any elaborate complaint.

jokes.text: "We're in Boogie Wonderland! Here we are at Boogie Wonderland and it is so much fun." — vampire's childlike delight at a cheesy nightclub
jokes.setup: The vampires and Nick have finally gotten into Boogie Wonderland
jokes.punchline: Viago's earnest joy at gaining entry to what is clearly a tacky Wellington nightclub is played completely straight — the contrast between ancient vampire and suburban nightclub enthusiasm is the joke
jokes.explanation: Functional fish-out-of-water joke. Viago's sincere enthusiasm for a mundane location is a character note, but it's not especially inventive compared to the reel's stronger moments.

jokes.text: "We're in Boogie Wonderland! Here we are at Boogie Wonderland and it is so much fun. This is amazing! I'm so happy to be here."
jokes.setup: The vampires have arrived at the nightclub
jokes.punchline: Viago narrates their arrival with the wonder of a tourist describing the Eiffel Tower — this is a mid-tier Wellington nightclub
jokes.explanation: Good character beat for Viago — his genuine delight at a mediocre nightclub is consistent with his centuries-old naivety about contemporary culture. Mild laugh.

jokes.text: "This is pretty cheesy. Also, did you see the jacket he wore? He's wearing the same jacket as me." — vampire complaint at nightclub
jokes.setup: The vampires are at Boogie Wonderland
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's critique of the nightclub pivots immediately to a petty jacket grievance — ancient vampire, timeless fashion anxiety
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — ancient vanity expressed through contemporary social anxiety. The pivot from nightclub critique to jacket complaint is a fun character non-sequitur.

jokes.text: "This is pretty cheesy. Also, did you see the jacket he wore? He's wearing the same jacket as me."
jokes.setup: The group is at Boogie Wonderland
jokes.punchline: Deacon's primary concern in a club full of potential victims is that someone has the same jacket as him
jokes.explanation: Mundane social anxiety from an ancient vampire. The vanity pivot is well-timed but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "I can smell werewolves. Okay, we're just about to walk past some werewolves so some shit might go down!"
jokes.setup: The group is walking through the nightclub area; Nick has picked up a scent
jokes.punchline: Nick's breathless, almost sports-commentary announcement that shit might go down — delivered with excitement rather than caution — reveals his immaturity as a vampire
jokes.explanation: Good Nick character beat — the excitement of a teenager stirring up drama. 'Some shit might go down' is very Nick. Character-integrated.

jokes.text: "Over there, is the big Fat Lady's Arms. Ah, on Wednesday's there be, like fear factor competition. You can win like t-shirts and hats and small prizes."
jokes.setup: Nick is orienting his vampire friends to the local nightlife
jokes.punchline: His tour guide information is aggressively prosaic — he describes the bar's Fear Factor competition and its 'small prizes' with tour-guide authority
jokes.explanation: Local flavour gag. The specificity of 't-shirts and hats and small prizes' is funny in its banality. Nick's earnestness about mediocre information is in character.

jokes.text: "Look out guys. Don't catch fleas." — Deacon's taunt at the werewolves
jokes.setup: The vampire group is walking past the werewolves; Deacon is posturing
jokes.punchline: 'Don't catch fleas' as a vampire insult to werewolves — the supernatural equivalent of a tired playground taunt, suggesting centuries of rivalry have produced only mediocre trash-talk
jokes.explanation: Decent setup for the werewolf confrontation. The flea taunt is appropriately weak and petty — which is the joke.

jokes.text: "We've got sensitive hearing." — werewolf's dignified response to overhearing the flea comment
jokes.setup: Deacon thinks he's gotten away with the taunt; the werewolves heard it
jokes.punchline: The werewolf's response — calmly announcing their sensitive hearing rather than immediately escalating — is a weirdly measured, almost HR-complaint tone that makes them more sympathetic than the vampires
jokes.explanation: Good character establishment for the werewolves as a contrast group — they respond to provocations calmly, with information rather than aggression. It recontextualizes them as the more mature party in the supernatural rivalry.

jokes.text: "We don't want any trouble." / "Why did you start it?" / "Well, I do. Have I got your hackles up?"
jokes.setup: The vampire group has accidentally provoked the werewolves and is trying to manage the situation
jokes.punchline: While Viago is trying to de-escalate, Deacon immediately contradicts him — he DOES want trouble
jokes.explanation: Good split-character comedy. The vampires can't present a unified front even during a confrontation. 'Have I got your hackles up?' is an appropriately dog-pun-adjacent taunt.

jokes.text: "We don't smell our own crutches. We smell each other's crutches. And it's a... form of... greeting."
jokes.setup: Deacon has made another crotch-sniffing jab at the werewolves
jokes.punchline: The werewolf leader calmly corrects the misconception — they don't smell their OWN, they smell EACH OTHER'S, and then has to explain with great gravity that it's 'a form of greeting', as if reading from a cultural sensitivity document
jokes.explanation: Very well constructed. The distinction between self-smelling and mutual-smelling is both absurd and weirdly logical, and the leader explaining it with the grave dignity of someone defending a cultural practice is perfect character work. 'It's a... form of... greeting' with the pauses suggests he knows how it sounds but insists on its legitimacy.

jokes.text: "It's Count Fagula." — werewolf insults Vladislav; followed by "Hey, hey, hey! Don't swear."
jokes.setup: The vampire-werewolf confrontation is escalating; a werewolf throws an insult
jokes.punchline: Anton — the werewolf leader — immediately reprimands his pack member for swearing, with more urgency than the actual insult provoked. The werewolves have an internal swearing rule that supersedes aggression.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the werewolves-not-swearwolves payoff coming. Anton's immediate disciplinary intervention — prioritizing the no-swearing rule over the vampire insult — establishes the werewolves as a pack with internal codes that are more important to them than external conflicts.

jokes.text: "We're werewolves, not swearwolves." — Anton corrects his pack member
jokes.setup: A werewolf swore during the confrontation; Anton has been scolding them about not swearing
jokes.punchline: The pack responds in unison: 'We're werewolves, not swearwolves' — a pack mantra that is simultaneously a terrible pun and a perfectly absurd statement of group identity
jokes.explanation: The best joke in this reel and among the best in the film. 'We're werewolves, not swearwolves' works on every level: it's a great pun, it's delivered as a group MANTRA (suggesting they've said this before, have a whole pack culture around it), it establishes the werewolves as a comedic foil with more internal dignity than the vampires, and the earnestness with which Anton says it is absolutely key. It's the kind of line that makes audiences immediately want to repeat it. Earns 9+ on character integration because it could ONLY work in this context — no other character type could deliver this with this meaning. Approaches the craft anchor for best lines in comedy television.

jokes.text: "Well, at least you're talking about a bundle of sticks." — vampire's response to being called a homophobic slur; followed by "Please, this bundle of sticks..."
jokes.setup: The werewolf has used a homophobic insult as the vampire's nickname
