jokes.punchline: Instead of responding to the slur, the vampires pivot to the word's archaic meaning — discussing the actual bundle-of-sticks etymology with apparent sincerity — refusing to engage with the intended insult
jokes.explanation: Good deflection gag — the vampires respond to the slur by being etymologically pedantic, which sidesteps the intended sting. The 'bundle of sticks' discussion as a sincere rebuttal works well, though it's a relatively common comedic move.

jokes.text: "No, listen, that's offensive... We're a really offensive word to call people." — vampires continuing to object to the slur
jokes.setup: The confrontation continues with the werewolves defending the slur as 'just a bundle of sticks'
jokes.punchline: The vampires are more offended by the language than by the actual threat of violence
jokes.explanation: Extension of the decorum joke. The 'bundle of sticks' etymology defence is a real-world internet argument transplanted into a supernatural context, which is a good meta-joke, though slightly over-explained.

jokes.text: "Do the breathing! Do the breathing. Count to 10, mate. Count to 10. Count to 10, human again."
jokes.setup: A werewolf is about to transform in anger
jokes.punchline: Anton's de-escalation technique for a werewolf mid-transformation is a breathing exercise and counting to ten — the most mundane anger management therapy applied to supernatural creature management
jokes.explanation: Very well done. 'Count to 10, human again' is the killer phrase — the goal of the breathing exercise is to remain human. The domestication of werewolf anger management through a preschool technique is rich character comedy and reveals an entire internal culture of the werewolf pack.

jokes.text: "Thanks a lot guys. You should be ashamed of yourselves, man." — Anton reprimanding the vampires after de-escalating his pack
jokes.setup: The confrontation is over; Anton has successfully calmed his pack
jokes.punchline: Anton addresses the vampires with the disappointed tone of a school principal — placing moral responsibility on them for provoking his pack, while he remains the composed adult in the room
jokes.explanation: Good character note — Anton's moral authority over the entire encounter (vampires AND his own pack) is a consistent and funny inversion of the expected dynamic.

jokes.text: "Say it! Don't spray it, bitch!" — Deacon gets a last word in; "Declan! Why are you swearing all the time?!"
jokes.setup: The werewolves are walking away; Deacon shouts a parting insult
jokes.punchline: Anton pivots immediately from addressing the vampires to scolding his pack member for swearing — 'bitch' has triggered the no-swearing protocol again, mid-retreat
jokes.explanation: Perfect running gag callback. The werewolves' no-swearing rule gets the last laugh — their own exit is interrupted by an internal infraction. 'Why are you swearing all the time?!' suggests this is a chronic problem for Declan specifically, adding depth to the pack dynamic.

jokes.text: Nick's confessional about telling Stu he's a vampire: lengthy, sincere buildup about not knowing how to approach it
jokes.setup: Nick has been building to telling Stu about vampires with great seriousness
jokes.punchline: The gravity of the confessional (how DO you tell a friend you're a vampire?) is itself the joke — Nick treating this like a coming-out conversation or a medical diagnosis reveal
jokes.explanation: Setup for the subsequent joke. As a standalone moment it's functional but runs a bit long — it's mostly setup scaffolding.

jokes.text: Nick's vampire-coming-out conversation with Stu: leading evidence includes "I don't show up for lunch anymore" and "changed the story of Tina's games"
jokes.setup: Nick is building his case that something has changed before delivering the vampire reveal
jokes.punchline: His evidence for his supernatural transformation consists entirely of minor lifestyle changes — not showing up for lunch, changed Tina game outcomes — which both dramatize and miniaturize the revelation
jokes.explanation: Good cringe-comedy structure — Nick doing a dramatic 'you must have noticed' buildup with extremely pedestrian evidence. The 'Tina's games' detail (which we can't fully parse) adds absurdist texture.

jokes.text: "You probably noticed, it has been... I've been going through a few changes lately." — Nick's coming-out-as-vampire speech
jokes.setup: Nick is building up to telling Stu he's a vampire
jokes.punchline: He frames becoming an immortal blood-drinking predator as 'going through a few changes lately' — as if it were puberty or a career pivot
jokes.explanation: The euphemism works well. 'Going through a few changes' is exactly how someone would phrase a difficult but mundane revelation, which makes vampirism feel charmingly small-scale.

jokes.text: "So... The reason I brought you here... is to tell you that... I'm a vampire." — Nick's big reveal to Stu
jokes.setup: Nick has built up to this revelation with enormous gravity; Stu has been responding with 'yeah' to all the evidence
jokes.punchline: The reveal itself — 'I'm a vampire' — is delivered with the solemnity of a coming-out moment, while Stu's reaction (implied: calm acceptance) deflates it completely
jokes.explanation: The punchline here is mostly Stu's reaction (taking it very well) rather than the reveal itself, which is straight. Functional but the comedy lands in what comes after.

jokes.text: "Stu took it pretty well... But if they ever offer you bisghetti... Um... you shouldn't eat it."
jokes.setup: Nick is debriefing after the vampire reveal; Stu has apparently accepted it calmly
jokes.punchline: His practical advice for Stu about navigating vampire social life is: avoid the bisghetti. After all the supernatural revelation, the most useful thing he can say is about the worm-pasta.
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback. After a dramatic supernatural revelation, Nick's most useful protective advice for his friend is to avoid the worm-pasta. The word 'bisghetti' has been fully absorbed into his vocabulary now. The gap between the supernatural stakes (you're now in a vampire house) and the practical warning (avoid the pasta) is perfectly calibrated. The best use of the bisghetti running gag.

jokes.text: "They offered me biscotti." — Stu's response (apparently he was offered something different)
jokes.setup: Nick has just warned Stu about bisghetti; Stu reveals he was offered biscotti
jokes.punchline: The deflation — Stu got the mundane Italian snack, not the worm-pasta — either suggests the vampires were more polite to Stu or simply didn't do the prank on him. Either interpretation is funny.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — one word (biscotti) does all the work. The substitution of an actually Italian snack for the vampire's worm-pasta prank is a great small joke. Stu is apparently already getting better treatment than Nick did.

jokes.text: "Vampire mates don't eat human mates. And no matter how much I want to eat him... I will never eat him cause he's my mate. Right, Stu?" / "Yah."
jokes.setup: Nick is making an earnest pledge not to eat Stu
jokes.punchline: He asks Stu to confirm the agreement and Stu simply, calmly says 'Yah' — as if this is a normal friendship pact
jokes.explanation: Good sustained dark comedy. The 'Right, Stu?' confirmation is a great touch — Nick needs Stu's buy-in on the 'don't eat him' agreement, and Stu gives it without drama. Their friendship dynamic is established here as genuinely sweet and deeply weird simultaneously.

jokes.text: "We really like him. At first I wanted to kill him. But now I'm glad I've spent the time to get to know him."
jokes.setup: The vampires are discussing Stu in confessionals
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's progression from 'wanted to kill him' to 'glad I took the time' mirrors exactly the arc of a friend group accepting a new person — except it starts from homicide
jokes.explanation: Very well structured. The beat-for-beat correspondence between this and a normal 'getting to know someone' confession is what makes it land — 'at first I wanted to kill him, but...' tracks perfectly with 'at first I wasn't sure about him, but...' The sincerity of the final sentiment makes it genuinely warm AND funny simultaneously.

jokes.text: "Yeah, of course he looks delicious with his big red cheeks."
jokes.setup: Viago is explaining why Stu is well-liked by the vampire house
jokes.punchline: His warm description of Stu pivots immediately to 'he looks delicious with his big red cheeks' — genuine affection and predatory appetite expressed in one breath
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Nick's 'reddest guy I know' beat — the vampires consistently perceive Stu through an appetitive lens even while genuinely befriending him. 'Big red cheeks' as the specific appealing feature is nicely specific.

jokes.text: "But we've all got an agreement that we're not going to eat Stu." — followed by unanimous 'Right?' / 'Right.'
jokes.setup: The vampires have been confessing how delicious Stu looks
jokes.punchline: There is a formal pact — apparently necessary — that nobody will eat Stu. The 'Right? Right.' loop of confirmation suggests this agreement requires constant reaffirmation.
jokes.explanation: The formal vampire pact about not eating a friend is a good sustained dark comedy note. The 'Right?' ritual suggests the temptation is ongoing and the pact needs active maintenance.

jokes.text: "That's ... it started off with, 'Who's this human you're bringing into the house?' But it took them literally 2 minutes and they like him more than they like me, I reckon."
jokes.setup: Nick is describing how the vampires received Stu
jokes.punchline: The vampires who tried to murder him — and reluctantly let him in — have adopted his friend faster than they accepted Nick himself. Nick is jealous.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Nick's jealousy about Stu being immediately accepted while he's still on probation is a natural and funny dynamic. The 'literally 2 minutes' specificity is good.

jokes.text: "I'm knitting a scarf for Stu." — Deacon, in confessional
jokes.setup: Various vampires are expressing their fondness for Stu
jokes.punchline: Deacon — the most aggressive and vain of the vampires — has apparently been knitting Stu a scarf as a gift. The domesticity of this from a centuries-old predator who was recently trying to murder Nick is the joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the best small jokes in the reel. Five words. Deacon — who was engineering murder schemes with bisghetti and snake-penis hexes — has been knitting. The domestic tenderness from the most aggressive character is perfectly incongruous. The specificity of 'a scarf' (not just a gift — a scarf he's knitting himself) makes it even better. Near-8 level for economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Nick teaching Deacon to use a computer / Deacon asking about a crucifix in the background of a photo
jokes.setup: Nick is apparently trying to teach the vampires modern technology
jokes.punchline: Deacon is distracted by a crucifix in a photo background, suggesting the mundane challenge of internet browsing is impossible when you're being distracted by symbols of your own vulnerability
jokes.explanation: Good concept — crucifix phobia as a barrier to internet use — but the transcript is sparse here and the actual visual comedy is hard to fully reconstruct. Probably funnier on screen.

jokes.text: Nick pleads with Petyr not to turn Stu into a vampire: 'He's a vegetarian. Last thing he'd want to is eat a life-being or eat blood or eat meat...'
jokes.setup: Nick is worried Petyr will attack Stu like he attacked Nick
jokes.punchline: His argument against Stu becoming a vampire is that he's a vegetarian — as if dietary ethics would be the main obstacle to accepting immortality
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Nick's protective instinct expressed through the most practical concern he can articulate. Vegetarianism as an argument against vampirism is a funny and character-consistent angle.

jokes.text: "I've lost... a really nice silk scarf in about 1912." — vampire Googling lost possessions
jokes.setup: Nick is teaching the vampires to use Google/the internet
jokes.punchline: Vladislav immediately uses the internet to search for a scarf he lost in 1912 — his primary use-case for the most powerful information tool in human history is recovering century-old property
jokes.explanation: Excellent. The specificity of '1912' makes it real — this is an actual unresolved grievance for him. The juxtaposition of the internet's infinite potential and Vladislav's one use (finding his lost scarf from 112 years ago) is perfect. The year-specificity is the detail that elevates it.

jokes.text: "Stu is the first human friend that I've had for a long time. With humans there's a tendency to die."
jokes.setup: Vladislav is discussing his emotional relationship with Stu
jokes.punchline: 'With humans there's a tendency to die' — delivered as a mild inconvenience, as if human mortality is a design flaw that makes long-term friendship with them administratively annoying
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the reel. 'With humans there's a tendency to die' is a perfect deadpan encapsulation of the vampire's eternal perspective — human mortality viewed as a character flaw rather than a tragedy. The phrasing 'a tendency to die' (as if it's an unfortunate habit, like being late) is exquisitely calibrated. High originality, perfect economy, and a highly quotable line that could only come from an immortal being. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: "Or you can poke her." — vampire interpreting Facebook's 'poke' feature
jokes.setup: Nick is showing Vladislav someone's Facebook page
jokes.punchline: The Facebook 'poke' feature takes on predatory/literal significance when introduced to a vampire — the ambiguity of whether Vladislav understands the digital feature or is interpreting it as physical contact with a potential victim
jokes.explanation: Good concept — the 'poke' feature read literally by a vampire is a nice piece of tech-vampire comedy. The ambiguity is the humor. Somewhat dated (Facebook poke is already nostalgic) but works in context.

jokes.text: "Can we see a movie with sunrise?" — vampire requesting to watch sunrise footage online
jokes.setup: The vampires are exploring what they can find on the internet
jokes.punchline: Viago's request to see a movie with a sunrise — the one thing that would kill him — delivered as innocent curiosity is both sweet and darkly funny
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. The childlike wonder of 'can we see a sunrise?' from someone who can never see one in life is simultaneously poignant and funny. Viago's gentle character is perfectly served by this request.

jokes.text: "Can we see a movie with sunrise?" — vampire asks to watch sunrise footage
jokes.setup: The vampires are exploring the internet with Nick's guidance
jokes.punchline: Viago's first request — to see a sunrise — reveals what an immortal being who can never safely experience it would most want from the internet: the one thing his condition permanently denies him
jokes.explanation: Beautiful small joke with unexpected emotional depth. The internet becomes the vampire's window to the experience of daylight — genuinely touching and funny simultaneously. The 'What? Shit!' reaction (presumably Viago recoiling from the brightness of sunrise imagery on a screen) is a perfect physical beat.

jokes.text: "What? Shit!" / "Whoo..." — vampire recoils from sunrise images on screen
jokes.setup: Viago has asked to see a sunrise on the computer
jokes.punchline: He apparently recoils as if physically burned by the image of sunlight on a screen — his vampire physiology confused by the digital representation of his greatest threat
jokes.explanation: Good visual payoff for the sunrise joke. The vampire's visceral reaction to digital sunlight (his instincts unable to distinguish screen from sky) is both logical within the fiction and perfectly absurd. Stronger as a visual gag than as transcript.

jokes.text: "If you push images, then we can see pictures of virgins." — vampire's search term suggestion
jokes.setup: The vampires are exploring Google Images
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's first thought for what to search is 'virgins' — his entire internet use-case is food-sourcing — and he believes this is a plausible search term that will yield useful results
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the virgin blood discussion from earlier in the reel (joke 5-6). The practical food-sourcing approach to internet search is a nice extension of the vampire's alien perspective on technology.

jokes.text: "I don't think she's a virgin if she's doing that." — vampire assessing search results
jokes.setup: Vladislav has searched for virgins on Google Images; they are looking at results
jokes.punchline: His clinical assessment of image results for virgin status — delivered as sober quality-control — applies predatory criteria to internet pornography (implied) with absolute straight-faced earnestness
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the virgins search. The earnest quality-assessment of internet imagery for vampire dining criteria is well-executed. The implication of what they've found is funnier than anything explicit.

jokes.text: "This is my old servant, Phillip. So, we're gonna call him... screen..." — vampire using Skype/video call for the first time
jokes.setup: Vladislav has found his old servant Phillip online, apparently an elderly man
jokes.punchline: The discovery of video calling is experienced as profound magic — 'we're gonna call him, screen...' — with the vampire not knowing the name of the technology he's using
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the final joke of the reel. The vampire's fumbling with 'screen...' as the name for video calling is well-observed. Good character integration.

jokes.text: "My God, that's him, that's him, that's him, that's Phillip, that's Phillip. — He looks old."
jokes.setup: Vladislav has connected to his old servant Phillip via video call; he is overcome with emotion at seeing him
jokes.punchline: The observation — 'He looks old' — delivered about a human servant that the immortal vampire has presumably not seen in decades is a perfect deadpan. Of course he looks old. Only a vampire would experience this as a notable observation.
jokes.explanation: Superb closer for the reel. After the emotional buildup of Vladislav recognizing Phillip ('that's him, that's him!'), the flat observation 'He looks old' is a perfect deflation — and the entire joke only works because Vladislav is immortal. The point of view could ONLY be a vampire's: surprise that a human has aged. The structure (escalating excitement → flat observation) is immaculate, and the economy of three words closing the reel is excellent. Earns its 8.

jokes.text: Nick comparing himself to the Twilight protagonist while vampires around him react with bewilderment
jokes.setup: Nick has been newly turned and is bragging about being a vampire, invoking Twilight as a romantic frame of reference
jokes.punchline: 'I'm the main guy in Twilight. You know the main guy? That's me.' — the gap between how glamorous Nick thinks vampires are and how the ancient vampires see themselves is the core absurdity
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Nick's Twilight delusion perfectly encapsulates his character: a modern guy who romanticizes vampirism through pop culture instead of grasping its reality. The ancient vampires' disdain is implied and devastating. Character-integrated and funny on its own terms.

jokes.text: Nick casually admitting he has told random strangers — including a girl, her hot friend, and an unnamed man — that he is a vampire
jokes.setup: The vampires confront Nick about telling humans he's a vampire; they expect maybe one slip
jokes.punchline: Nick keeps casually revealing more and more people he's told: 'I told her hot friend... Who's that guy? I don't know but I told him.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating structure is clean: each new revelation is funnier than the last, culminating in Nick pointing at a stranger he doesn't even know. 'Who's that guy? I don't know but I told him' is an extremely efficient and funny line. Good economy, strong structure.

jokes.text: Nick explaining his 'eye condition' as 'vampire eyes' to a stranger, then casually flashing his fangs
jokes.setup: Nick is out in public and needs to explain his appearance; he calls it an 'eye condition'
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts the cover story by showing his fangs and saying 'I'm a vampire' with zero hesitation
jokes.explanation: Solid joke on Nick's obliviousness — he tries to hide it for one second and then immediately blows it. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'I'm a vampire hunter.' / 'No, you're not.' / 'No?' / 'You fucking piece of shit.'
jokes.setup: Nick tells a stranger he's a vampire; the stranger claims to be a vampire hunter
jokes.punchline: Nick dismisses the vampire hunter claim with casual contempt: 'No, you're not... You fucking piece of shit.' — the insult lands as the punchline because it's so disproportionate
jokes.explanation: The abrupt pivot to insult is funny and efficient. The deadpan 'No, you're not' followed by an expletive is classic comedy economy. The irony — Nick is correct, but entirely for the wrong reasons — adds a layer.

jokes.text: 'I'll Skype you!' — the stranger yells this as he's being confronted by vampires
jokes.setup: An intense confrontation between Nick and what turns out to be a real vampire hunter
jokes.punchline: The vampire hunter de-escalates with the most mundane modern farewell: 'I'll Skype you!'
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous comedic payoff. The bathos of a vampire hunter threatening to 'Skype you' in the middle of a supernatural confrontation is a perfect tonal collision. Very quotable and highly original in its brevity.

jokes.text: 'I float. I transform into stuff.' Nick boasting of abilities, then being immediately called out
jokes.setup: Nick is trying to impress people by demonstrating vampire powers
jokes.punchline: 'Don't lie about transforming into shit' — Vladislav cuts Nick down because Nick clearly cannot transform
jokes.explanation: The gap between Nick's boasting and his actual incompetence is the film's running engine. This is a clean instance of it, though not its funniest expression.

jokes.text: Beat/reaction — implied visual of Nick clearly unable to demonstrate any transformation, followed by silence and 'Don't lie about transforming into shit'
jokes.setup: Nick claims he can transform; everyone waits; nothing happens
jokes.punchline: The gap between the boast and the silence is the joke; Vladislav's flat rebuke confirms it
jokes.explanation: The gap from 42:00 to 42:21 is a visual comedy beat — nine seconds of presumably nothing happening before the rebuke. Classic awkward silence payoff in mockumentary style.

jokes.text: 'Twilight! Shut up, Nick!'
jokes.setup: Nick has been invoking Twilight as his vampire identity throughout the scene
jokes.punchline: One of the flatmates mockingly calls him 'Twilight' as a taunt; another snaps at him to shut up
jokes.explanation: A quick callback gag that lands modestly. The mockery is deserved and the rhythm is right, but it's a one-beat joke without additional twist.

jokes.text: The 'You shut up / No, you shut up' argument, culminating in 'I'm Dracula, man!' / 'You're not Dracula!'
jokes.setup: A confrontation about Nick's big mouth devolves into a petty shouting match
jokes.punchline: Nick's trump card in the argument is claiming to be Dracula; this is immediately disputed
jokes.explanation: The circular 'you shut up' escalation is a classic comedic spiral, and the sudden 'I'm Dracula' claim is a funny non-sequitur escalation that reveals Nick's desperate ego. Good energy.

jokes.text: 'Oh, bat fight! Bat fight! Oh, yah, yah, yah!'
jokes.setup: The vampire argument escalates to a physical confrontation; the vampires presumably transform into bats
jokes.punchline: Humans watching treat a supernatural bat-form brawl like a spectator sport, cheering with delight
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of an ancient supernatural confrontation being cheered on like a pub fight is delightful. 'Oh, bat fight!' has the cadence of 'oh, cat fight!' and the mundanity of that comparison is the joke. High energy and very funny on screen.

jokes.text: 'My fucking jacket, man!' Deacon's primary concern after a bat brawl is his jacket
jokes.setup: A supernatural brawl has just occurred with serious stakes
jokes.punchline: Deacon's post-fight concern is entirely about his ruined jacket, not the confrontation's outcome
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Deacon, whose vanity is established. The bathos of reducing a supernatural conflict to damaged clothing is a clean and efficient joke.

jokes.text: 'How's your worms? Alright. You're eating worms.'
jokes.setup: Post-brawl, the group checks in with Stu, the human friend; Vladislav's mesmerism has turned something Stu is eating into worms
jokes.punchline: The exchange is almost casual — 'You're eating worms' delivered as mild observation rather than alarm
jokes.explanation: The casualness is the joke. 'You're eating worms' as a simple statement of fact, and Stu responding with equanimity ('Alright'), captures the film's deadpan perfectly. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: 'Only works on things that already look like worms. Maybe noodles. Do you want some noodles?'
jokes.setup: Nick asks if the mesmerism works on chips
jokes.punchline: Vladislav explains the surprisingly specific constraint of his power ('only things that already look like worms') and immediately pivots to offering noodles as an alternative
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely exceptional joke writing. The constraint — 'only works on things that already look like worms' — is an absurdist rule delivered with complete sincerity, which makes the supernatural feel mundane and bureaucratic. The immediate 'maybe noodles. Do you want some noodles?' is the perfect hospitable pivot. It's funny on craft alone and deeply rewatchable. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its economy and originality.

jokes.text: Viago's 'Oh no. I wouldn't eat that' — reaction to Stu eating worm-chips
jokes.setup: Stu is eating something that has been transformed into worms
jokes.punchline: Viago's belated, mild, and entirely unhelpful advisory comment
jokes.explanation: The belated, polite-but-useless nature of the warning is Viago's character to a T. Modest laugh, decent economy.

jokes.text: Nick's lament: 'I can't eat salads now. I can't sunbathe. I can't watch daytime TV... My favorite food. I can't eat chips. I hate... I said it. I'm over being a vampire. It's shit. Don't believe the hype.'
jokes.setup: Nick has been newly vampirized and is coming to terms with the downsides
jokes.punchline: His list of losses escalates from relatively sensible (sunbathing) to absurd ('I can't eat chips') to deflatingly mundane — culminating in 'I'm over being a vampire. It's shit. Don't believe the hype.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in this reel. 'Don't believe the hype' applied to vampirism is an unexpected, perfectly modern phrase that punctures centuries of gothic mythology. The build through petty losses (chips!) to existential disappointment is structurally excellent and deeply character-specific. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Jackie's domestic frustration: 'You know if I had a penis, I would have been bitten years ago'
jokes.setup: Jackie is Deacon's human familiar who does chores and has been waiting to be turned into a vampire; she's being told it's delayed again because of Nick
jokes.punchline: She identifies the homoerotic, male-centric nature of vampire recruitment as the reason for her exclusion
jokes.explanation: Sharp, dark, and character-specific. Jackie's bitterness about gender discrimination in vampire immortality is both funny and pointed. The line is specific enough to be unexpected and broad enough to resonate.

jokes.text: Jackie's rant: 'Like one big circle, just biting each other's dicks... a big homoerotic dick-biting club. And I'm stuck here, ironing their fucking frills.'
jokes.setup: Jackie continues her feminist critique of vampire society
jokes.punchline: The imagery escalates to 'biting each other's dicks' and then lands with brutal domesticity: 'ironing their fucking frills'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the standout moments in the reel. The escalation from gender discrimination to 'homoerotic dick-biting club' is shocking and funny, and the landing on 'ironing their fucking frills' is devastating in its mundane specificity. The word 'frills' — the ornate vampire collars — is a perfect choice that earns big laughs. Highly quotable, deeply character-integrated. Approaches 8.0 anchor quality.

jokes.text: Deacon's immediate follow-up after Jackie's rant: 'Also clean the bathroom, please. It's blood everywhere. It is gruesome. Okay, see you tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Jackie has just delivered an impassioned speech about being exploited
jokes.punchline: Deacon responds by adding more chores and signing off cheerfully, entirely ignoring her grievance
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing. The structure is flawless: Jackie's escalating fury, then Deacon airily adds 'Also clean the bathroom, please. It's blood everywhere. It is gruesome.' The 'it is gruesome' as an afterthought — with the implication that he's aware it's disgusting and doesn't care — is excellent. 'Okay, see you tomorrow' as a cheerful sign-off completes the cruelty. Earns a high score for structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Vladislav's talking-head about Katherine: 'Sure, I wanted to kill the guy. I thought about chopping his head off. Draining him of every drop of blood... Who wouldn't?' — delivered as if describing a relatable jealous feeling
jokes.setup: Vladislav describes finding out his love interest was married
jokes.punchline: 'Sure, I wanted to kill the guy. I thought about chopping his head off... Who wouldn't?' — a completely normal jealousy narrative suddenly revealed as literal murderous intent, normalized with 'who wouldn't?'
jokes.explanation: Classic WWDITS move: vampire describes murderous impulses in the register of normal human relationship feelings. 'Who wouldn't?' is the key line — it assumes the audience shares the impulse, which is funny and slightly disturbing. Well-structured misdirection.

jokes.text: Petyr's death — a 8,000-year-old vampire killed by sunlight from a broken window in his own house
jokes.setup: Petyr is the oldest, most monstrous vampire in the flat; a vampire hunter has broken in
jokes.punchline: The ancient creature, survivor of millennia, is killed by accidental sunlight from a broken window in a Wellington flatmate situation — the mundanity of the death is the joke
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is structural and dark: an 8,000-year-old creature of the night dying in a messy flatmate dispute because a human told someone he was a vampire. The chain of absurd causality is very funny, and the chaos of the rescue attempt ('Get water! Get water!') adds physical comedy.

jokes.text: 'Our friend had just been killed in a fatal sunlight accident.'
jokes.setup: Petyr has just been burned alive by sunlight
jokes.punchline: Viago describes it with the bureaucratic language of a workplace injury report: 'a fatal sunlight accident'
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. 'Fatal sunlight accident' is a perfect piece of bureaucratic understatement applied to a vampire death. The phrase is both completely logical for a vampire and deeply absurd to a human ear. It's the kind of line that becomes a fan-quoted moment. Exceptional economy — four words do enormous work. Justifies 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Vladislav's crime scene reconstruction — treating Petyr's death like a police procedural while pointing to a table leg as the murder weapon
jokes.setup: Vladislav is trying to reconstruct what happened during the vampire hunter's attack
jokes.punchline: He delivers a full CSI-style analysis, holds up a table leg and says 'Think this is just a table leg, which is... sanded down. Do you think he hand sanded that?'
jokes.explanation: The genre parody here is sharp — treating a vampire slaying like a detective investigation, complete with forensic interest in the craftsmanship of the stake ('did he hand sand that?'). The question itself is funny because it's so off-topic given the horror of the situation.

jokes.text: 'Cover the crucifix!' — mid-reconstruction, Vladislav suddenly notices a crucifix and panics
jokes.setup: Vladislav is in the middle of a calm forensic explanation
jokes.punchline: His cool detective persona is instantly shattered by a reflexive panic over a crucifix in the room
jokes.explanation: Good comic interruption — the detective role-play is broken by an involuntary vampire weakness. The contrast between Vladislav's composed narration and sudden 'Cover the crucifix!' is funny and well-timed.

jokes.text: Nick reveals he told the vampire hunter (now dead) that he was a vampire — 'I thought he was joking. He said he was a vampire hunter.'
jokes.setup: The vampires are trying to identify the vampire hunter; Nick recognizes him
jokes.punchline: Nick admitted earlier he told a stranger who claimed to be a vampire hunter — now that stranger is dead in their basement and killed Petyr. The callback confirms the worst.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the earlier escalation joke. 'I thought he was joking' is devastating in context — Nick's naivety has caused a death. The structure rewards the earlier setup beautifully. Dark and funny.

jokes.text: 'You let a vampire hunter into our house?' / 'I just gave him my e-mail.' / 'Nick!' / 'Take out your tongue and shove it down your ass.'
jokes.setup: Nick has just confessed to giving his email to the vampire hunter who killed Petyr
jokes.punchline: 'Take out your tongue and shove it down your ass' — an absurdly specific and physically impossible insult delivered in total fury
jokes.explanation: The insult is completely original and physically absurd — 'take out your tongue and shove it down your ass' is not a standard insult, which makes it funnier. The specificity of the anatomy involved implies genuine ancient vampire rage. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'Get up and stand on this ceiling like a man.'
jokes.setup: Nick has presumably cowered or collapsed after being yelled at
jokes.punchline: 'Stand on this ceiling like a man' — the vampire version of 'man up' involves levitating to the ceiling, which recontextualizes human idiom through supernatural rules
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. 'Stand on this ceiling like a man' is a perfect economy joke: it takes a human expression ('stand up like a man') and replaces one word to reveal the vampire worldview completely. It's original, it's specific to the character and world, it's quotable, and it's short. This is joke writing at a high level. Justified 8+ score.

jokes.text: 'Get up and stand on this ceiling like a man.'
jokes.setup: Nick is cowering after being accused; Vladislav is trying to shame him into facing the consequences
jokes.punchline: The vampire version of 'man up' is 'stand on this ceiling like a man' — a standard shame tactic filtered through supernatural vampire capabilities
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in this entire reel. The construction is immaculate — it takes the universal human concept of 'man up / face this like an adult' and translates it perfectly into vampire idiom. 'Stand on this ceiling like a man' works because it's both logical within the vampire world (they can walk on ceilings) and absolutely absurd to human ears. The economy is superb. It's highly quotable, deeply character-specific to a world of vampires, and genuinely original. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor benchmark — this is an 8.5.

jokes.text: 'We can talk it out, yeah, man?' / 'We can talk it out, mate!' / 'I'll kill you!' / 'I'm already dead!'
jokes.setup: Deacon is furious and chasing Nick; Nick tries to de-escalate verbally
jokes.punchline: 'I'll kill you!' — 'I'm already dead!' — the threat of murder is literally meaningless as a threat to a vampire
jokes.explanation: Excellent deployment of the vampire's literal immortality as a punchline. The escalation into 'I'll kill you!' being immediately deflated by 'I'm already dead!' is clean, fast, and deeply funny. The logic is airtight and the economy is superb.

jokes.text: Police arriving and asking about 'a rather large amount of shrieking'
jokes.setup: An ancient vampire flat has just had a death, a bat brawl, and a murder; police arrive
jokes.punchline: The police describe the disturbance as 'a rather large amount of shrieking' — a massive understatement for supernatural chaos
jokes.explanation: Decent setup for the extended police scene. The British/NZ understatement of 'a rather large amount of shrieking' for what has been an insane supernatural night is funny but not exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Viago describes the smell as 'barbecue' when police comment on the odor — which is Petyr's burned corpse
jokes.setup: Police smell something odd in the vampire house; they ask what it is
jokes.punchline: 'Barbecue' — Petyr's charred remains are described as a barbecue
jokes.explanation: Single word punchline. The economy is near-perfect: everything the audience knows — the death, the charred remains, the horror — collapses into 'barbecue.' Dark, efficient, and very funny.

jokes.text: Police: 'Smells a bit weird here too, mate.' Vampire: 'Barbecue.'
jokes.setup: The police are walking through the vampires' house, smelling the aftermath of Petyr's immolation.
jokes.punchline: 'Barbecue.' — delivered flatly as a one-word explanation for the smell of an ancient vampire burning. It's both technically accurate and an absurd cover story.
jokes.explanation: One word. That's the whole joke. 'Barbecue.' delivered as a flat explanation for vampire immolation is a perfect one-word deadpan gag. Maximum economy (literally cannot be shorter), excellent structure (the question perfectly sets it up), and the word 'barbecue' has an almost cheerful quality that makes the dark truth funnier. This matches the 8.0 anchor quality.

jokes.text: Viago hypnotizes the police: 'You will not notice anything out of the ordinary' — cops respond 'No, we certainly hope not. Let's just keep going.'
jokes.setup: Viago attempts hypnosis on the police to cover up the supernatural chaos
jokes.punchline: The police reply as if they're following the instruction on its own terms — 'we certainly hope not' — implying the hypnosis works but also that NZ cops just don't want to find anything weird
jokes.explanation: The ambiguity is funny — are the cops hypnotized, or are they just stereotypically laid-back NZ police who don't want trouble? The joke works on both levels.

jokes.text: Viago's confessional: 'I'm not a great hypnotizer so it could wear off any second' — said while cops are still in the house
jokes.setup: The police are being led around the vampire house under hypnosis
jokes.punchline: Viago breaks to confess to the camera that he's actually bad at hypnosis and it might fail at any moment — adding real tension played for laughs
jokes.explanation: The mockumentary aside works well — Viago's charming incompetence is a consistent character note, and the aside creates genuine comedic tension.

jokes.text: Police discovering fire safety violations — no smoke detectors, indoor barbecue — and treating this as the primary concern
jokes.setup: Police are walking through a house with a burned vampire corpse, a murdered vampire hunter, and supernatural chaos
jokes.punchline: Their biggest concern is fire safety: 'Rule number 1: Smoke detectors. Rule number 2: maybe not so many barbecues inside.'
jokes.explanation: The genre inversion is excellent: horror movie house becomes a fire safety inspection. The cops reciting 'Rule Number 1' about smoke detectors while standing next to supernatural evidence is a great sustained joke. The hypnotism makes this doubly funny.

jokes.text: 'What kind of marinade?' — police asking about Petyr's charred remains mistaken for a barbecue
jokes.setup: Viago said the smell was 'barbecue'; now a cop is engaging with that explanation earnestly
jokes.punchline: 'What kind of marinade?' — the cop is genuinely interested in the recipe for the charred 8,000-year-old vampire
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'barbecue' is excellent, and the cop's follow-up question is perfect in its earnest domesticity. 'What kind of marinade?' applied to a burned vampire corpse is both horrific and hilarious. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Police finding the dead vampire hunter ('drunk guy') and lecturing about leaving party guests unattended
jokes.setup: The police encounter a dead vampire hunter in the basement
jokes.punchline: 'Mate, you're alright?' / 'He's drunk.' / 'That's what I thought.' — cops accept the explanation; then lecture about not leaving drunk people alone on cold concrete
jokes.explanation: The cops' reasonable, pastoral concern for a 'drunk guest' who is actually a dead vampire hunter is very funny. 'He's gonna feel terrible tomorrow morning' — the understatement about a dead person — is a great dark line.

jokes.text: 'Well, his soul is in hell, so...' / 'Well, I don't know where his soul's at, but all I am saying, where is his blanket?'
jokes.setup: Police are concerned about the welfare of the 'drunk' man (dead vampire hunter) on the concrete floor
jokes.punchline: Vladislav mentions the soul is in hell; cop ignores the metaphysical and just asks about the blanket
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. Vladislav casually mentioning 'his soul is in hell' and the cop completely sidestepping it to focus on the blanket is a masterwork of comedic collision. The cop's priorities are perfect — practical welfare concerns trump all metaphysics. 'I don't know where his soul's at, but where is his blanket?' is one of the funniest lines in the film and a contender for the best in this reel. Justified 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Police finding more fire hazards (adhesive near a lamp) and declaring 'That is quite bad. It's very bad.' while ignoring dead body
jokes.setup: Cops continue their tour of the horror house under hypnosis
jokes.punchline: Adhesive near a lamp gets graver concern than a corpse on the floor
jokes.explanation: Extension of the fire safety running gag. Solid but not as funny as the first instance; diminishing returns on the same joke.

jokes.text: 'Let's kill them.' / 'Well, let's just see what other safety...' — Deacon's quiet suggestion to murder the cops, casually deflected
jokes.setup: The police are leaving after their tour; the vampires deliberate
jokes.punchline: Deacon suggests killing them; Vladislav deflects with 'well, let's just see what other safety recommendations they have'
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'let's kill them' as a minor suggestion and the equally casual practical deflection is very much in the film's register. Vladislav's counter-suggestion treating murder as a less pressing option than fire safety notes is perfect.

jokes.text: 'Let's kill them.' / 'Well, let's just see what other safety...' — Vladislav suggesting murdering the police mid-safety-inspection
jokes.setup: The police are wrapping up their fire safety inspection. The vampires have been holding it together.
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's flat suggestion to kill the cops is treated by Viago as an equal-weight option to waiting for them to leave — the casual normalization of murder as a problem-solving option, balanced against seeing what other safety concerns they raise
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'Let's kill them' as a suggestion and Viago's equivocal response ('let's see what other safety concerns they have first') is funny. Murder as an administrative option, weighed against paperwork, is good vampire comedy.

jokes.text: The 'Trial of Nick' — formally convened vampire tribunal for flatmate grievances
jokes.setup: The vampires hold a formal trial for Nick's transgressions
jokes.punchline: The grandiosity of calling it 'this trial of Nick, of Wellington' in solemn council-speak for a flatmate dispute about telling people he's a vampire
jokes.explanation: The concept itself is funny — ancient vampires holding a solemn tribunal about flatmate behavior. 'Trial of Nick, of Wellington' is delightfully pompous for a dispute that boils down to house rules.

jokes.text: Crime 1: 'You brought a human into our house — which is a big no-no in the vampire world.' Then: 'Stu is okay though?' / 'Yeah, Stu is fine, I guess we'll just cross that one out.'
jokes.setup: First charge at the vampire trial: bringing a human into the house
jokes.punchline: The charge is immediately dropped because everyone likes Stu — 'we'll just cross that one out'
jokes.explanation: The formal tribunal immediately collapsing because everyone loves Stu is very funny. 'We'll just cross that one out' in solemn proceedings reveals the vampires are as susceptible to social favoritism as anyone. The irony that Stu is the only person they like undercuts their menace perfectly.

jokes.text: Crime number 1 (bringing a human into the house) is crossed off because 'Stu is okay though?' — and the charge is dismissed
jokes.setup: The formal charge is read: Nick brought a human into the house, 'which is a big no-no in the vampire world.'
jokes.punchline: The charge is immediately dropped because Stu — who is universally beloved — is fine. The gravity of the trial collapses instantly because everyone loves Stu. 'Thank you Stu.'
jokes.explanation: Stu's silent power over the vampires — his mere existence causes them to drop charges — is an ongoing comic thread. The gravity of a formal vampire trial deflating immediately because of one beloved human is excellent situational comedy. 'Thank you Stu' said in unison has great warmth.

jokes.text: Crime 2 reordering: 'That should have been crime number one but we wanted to build up to that.'
jokes.setup: The vampire tribunal is reading charges; they acknowledge the ordering is for dramatic effect
jokes.punchline: Vladislav admits mid-proceeding that they arranged the charges for narrative build-up, not by severity
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke about narrative structure — the vampires are aware of pacing, which is simultaneously self-aware and in-character for immortal beings who've seen a lot of drama. Good economy.

jokes.text: Crime 3: 'Deacon doesn't like that you wear the same jacket as him and he would like you to find your own original style.'
jokes.setup: The tribunal has covered a vampire's death and reckless endangerment of the flat
jokes.punchline: The final crime, delivered with equal gravity, is wearing the same jacket as Deacon — a petty fashion grievance amid genuine catastrophes
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation and callback. The tribunal has just covered a death, vampire exposure, and vampire hunter assassination — and the third official crime is a jacket dispute. Delivered with the same solemnity as the others. Deacon's vanity being codified into formal vampire law is excellent character comedy. One of the standout jokes in the reel.

jokes.text: Nick: 'So I can come back?' / Vladislav: 'No, indefinitely means there is no end.' / Nick: 'I thought...' / Vladislav: 'No, indefinite means it's not a definite thing.'
jokes.setup: Nick is told he is banished 'indefinitely' and misunderstands the word
jokes.punchline: Nick thinks 'indefinitely' means 'not definitively' (i.e., maybe temporary); Vladislav attempts to correct him while also not being entirely clear himself
jokes.explanation: The linguistic confusion is funny on multiple levels: Nick's misunderstanding is plausible (indefinitely IS ambiguous in casual usage) and Vladislav's correction isn't entirely wrong either. The escalating frustration adds energy.

jokes.text: 'But Stu, you can visit if you like.' / 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Nick is formally banished from the flat
jokes.punchline: The banishment is immediately modified to exclude Stu — everyone prefers Stu to Nick; the human is more welcome than the vampire
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Stu being universally beloved reaches a new height: Stu is explicitly welcome in a house from which a vampire has been banished. Stu's simple 'Thank you' is the perfect deadpan cap.

jokes.text: The Procession of Shame — vampires chanting 'Shame! Shame! Shame! Bad vampire!' while walking Nick out
jokes.setup: Nick is being banished; the punishment involves a 'procession of shame'
jokes.punchline: The procession consists of vampires chanting 'Shame! Shame! Bad vampire!' — a mix of medieval ritual and schoolyard scolding
jokes.explanation: The 'procession of shame' has the energy of a Game of Thrones reference ('shame, shame, shame' — the Walk of Atonement) collapsed into a flat dispute. 'Bad vampire!' is particularly funny — the register of scolding a pet applied to an immortal creature.

jokes.text: 'Bye Stu.' — Nick says a warm, genuine goodbye to Stu amid the shame procession
jokes.setup: Nick is being marched out in humiliation
jokes.punchline: He pauses to warmly say 'Bye Stu' — genuine affection breaking through the formal ritual
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny. The tone shift is genuine — Nick's friendship with Stu is the emotional note under the comedy. 'Bye Stu' is simple and effective.

jokes.text: 'That was a shame.' — Viago's post-procession reflection
jokes.setup: The procession of shame is over; Viago reflects
jokes.punchline: 'That was a shame' — a double meaning: both that it was a 'procession of shame' (literally) and that it was unfortunate (idiomatically)
jokes.explanation: Elegant wordplay in four words. 'That was a shame' works as both literal recap and emotional reflection. Near-perfect economy for a simple pun that lands on both levels. The deadpan delivery would make this land beautifully.

jokes.text: The Unholy Masquerade invitation described as burned on the edges 'like a treasure map or something'
jokes.setup: An elaborate invitation to the Unholy Masquerade arrives with singed edges
jokes.punchline: The vampires describe the dramatic invitation with the domestic enthusiasm of opening a party invite
jokes.explanation: Modest joke — the vampires' giddy excitement about the invitation contrasts with the dark aesthetic. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: The invitation lists co-sponsors: 'Wellington Vampire Association in conjunction with the lower-hat-vampire-witch club and the Kurory-zombie society'
jokes.setup: An elaborate Unholy Masquerade invitation is being read aloud
jokes.punchline: The coalition of evil includes bureaucratically named organizations: the 'lower-hat-vampire-witch club' — a community hall-style name for a coven
jokes.explanation: The bureaucratic naming of supernatural organizations — especially 'lower-hat-vampire-witch club' — is funny because it makes the undead world feel like a Wellington community notice board. Good worldbuilding comedy.

jokes.text: The start time of the Unholy Masquerade: 'Starting at 6 PM' — '666...' — 'Oh, yeah...'
jokes.setup: The masquerade starts at 6 PM on June 6th
jokes.punchline: They connect 6/6 at 6 PM to 666 with mild, unsurprised recognition — like spotting a familiar brand
jokes.explanation: Light and efficient. The 666 recognition being a mild 'oh yeah' rather than any kind of excitement is the joke — the supernatural is routine to them.

jokes.text: Viago confessional: 'One year I went to the Unholy Masquerade dressed as Whoopi Goldberg from Sister Act 1 and Sister Act 2: Back in the Habit. Didn't go down so well because she was a nun.'
jokes.setup: Viago talks about the importance of the Unholy Masquerade
jokes.punchline: His costume choice — a nun — was poorly received by vampires; crucifixes and nuns are lethal to them. The specific naming of both Sister Act films adds to the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the entire reel. The specificity of 'Whoopi Goldberg from Sister Act 1 and Sister Act 2: Back in the Habit' is already absurd and funny. The payoff — 'didn't go down so well because she was a nun' — is both logical within the vampire world and completely ridiculous in context. It has perfect character integration (Viago's earnest, well-meaning cluelessness), great structure, and high originality. Highly quotable and deeply rewatchable.

jokes.text: Vladislav's self-important rumor: 'I heard a little rumor that the guest of honor this year might be me' — delivered with false modesty
jokes.setup: Vladislav teases the camera about a rumor regarding the guest of honor
jokes.punchline: He builds suspense about the rumor and then reveals it's about himself — classic narcissistic reveal
jokes.explanation: In-character for Vladislav's narcissism, but the structure is predictable. The setup builds more than the punchline delivers.

jokes.text: Vladislav's reaction to learning 'The Beast' is the guest of honor — a long, wordless reaction shot as he processes the news
jokes.setup: Vladislav has convinced himself he's the guest of honor; the invitation names someone else
jokes.punchline: Long silent processing, followed by: 'Okay. Okay, that's fine. That's fine.' — the classic overcorrection of someone who is not fine
jokes.explanation: The 'that's fine, that's fine' overcorrection is a universal comedy beat — the person who insists they're okay when they clearly aren't. Character-specific to Vladislav's pride and history with The Beast.

jokes.text: Vladislav's reaction to learning The Beast is the guest of honor — a long pause, then 'Hm. Okay. Okay, that's fine. That's fine.' — clearly not fine
jokes.setup: The invitation reveals the guest of honor is The Beast — apparently Vladislav's greatest nemesis and trauma.
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's attempt to appear unbothered — 'Okay. Okay, that's fine. That's fine.' — with the camera holding on his clearly distressed face, is a classic deadpan reaction beat. The other character's aside ('Vladislav has just had a reaction') confirms what we're seeing.
jokes.explanation: The gap between 'that's fine' and clearly-not-fine is a well-executed reaction beat. The mockumentary format allows the camera to hold on the face, making the barely-suppressed panic funnier. Character-integrated: Vladislav has an enormous ego and meeting a greater nemesis is existentially threatening.

jokes.text: Multiple characters giving competing, increasingly dramatic descriptions of 'The Beast'
jokes.setup: The characters each try to describe The Beast to the documentarians
jokes.punchline: Everyone has a slightly different, increasingly hyperbolic description: 'The darkest part of my mind is reserved to The Beast... You should pray you never have to see The Beast... This one is called The Beast...'
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble comedy as each character adds to the Beast mythology. The structure of overlapping, competing accounts mimics documentary talking-head editing well.

jokes.text: Viago mockingly imitates Vladislav's Beast stories: 'I fought The Beast on a cliff.' 'I fought The Beast in a swamp.' 'One time I fought The Beast in the toilets of a nightclub.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav has told many dramatic stories about fighting The Beast
jokes.punchline: Viago mocks him by rattling off increasingly mundane and specific locations, culminating in 'the toilets of a nightclub'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from mythic settings (cliff, swamp) to 'the toilets of a nightclub' is perfectly structured. The final location collapses all the grandeur. The imitation format is well-executed and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Nick wants to go to the ball dressed as Blade — a vampire hunter — to a vampire party
jokes.setup: The vampires are discussing Unholy Masquerade costumes
jokes.punchline: 'You can't go to the ball as Blade. He's a vampire hunter.' / 'Yeah, but vampires love Wesley Snipes.'
jokes.explanation: 'Vampires love Wesley Snipes' is an excellent line — it's confident, specific, absurd, and perfectly in Nick's character (the new vampire who still has pop culture loyalties). The idea that the vampire community has an appreciation for the actor who played their most famous fictional hunter is rich and funny.

jokes.text: Vladislav paralyzed by indecision between pants options while having 'a mild crisis' about The Beast
jokes.setup: Vladislav is emotionally devastated about The Beast being guest of honor; everyone is trying to get ready
jokes.punchline: His crisis manifests as inability to choose between 'Green Jortes or the Black Leather with the Dragon Belt' — ancient vampire brought low by pants indecision
jokes.explanation: Vladislav's vanity and emotional turmoil colliding in a wardrobe crisis is good character comedy. 'Enough with the pants!' captures the exasperation well.

jokes.text: Viago tells Vladislav he looks terrible — 'you look terrible but if you ate someone on the way... you could probably wear a mask or something'
jokes.setup: Vladislav looks distressed and physically awful following the Beast news.
jokes.punchline: Viago's practical suggestion: eat someone on the way to the party to restore color to your complexion. 'You could probably wear a mask or something' — eating a person is option A, wearing a mask is an equivalent option B. The casual equivalence of murder with a cosmetic fix is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The casual normalization of murder as a beauty routine is consistent WWDITS territory. 'Eat someone on the way' as a pick-me-up recommendation, equal to 'wear a mask,' is good dark comedy.

jokes.text: 'Just leave me to do my dark bidding on the Internet!' / 'What are you bidding on?' / 'I'm bidding on a table.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav dramatically declares he'll stay home to do his 'dark bidding on the Internet'
jokes.punchline: 'What are you bidding on?' / 'I'm bidding on a table.' — the dark bidding is literally an eBay auction for furniture
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the reel and one of the great jokes in the film. 'Dark bidding on the Internet' sounds like a threat, possibly necromancy or some dark art. The misdirection is perfect — the question 'what are you bidding on?' is exactly what the audience is thinking. 'I'm bidding on a table' collapses all menace into pure domesticity in four words. The wordplay on 'bidding' (eBay bidding vs. dark bidding/command) is elegant. It earns its score by being both perfectly constructed and genuinely surprising. Comparable to 'Never go with a hippie to a second location' in its economy and surprise. The highest-impact joke in the reel.

jokes.text: Viago proudly displays his homemade mask at the Unholy Masquerade while introducing his human familiar Jackie as a vampire
jokes.setup: They are at an exclusive undead-only Unholy Masquerade, an apparently serious supernatural social event
jokes.punchline: Viago announces 'This is my mask. Which I made for the occasion.' — implying a proudly crafted but presumably amateurish DIY mask at what should be a grand gothic affair
jokes.explanation: Classic Viago naivety — his earnest pride in a probably terrible handmade mask at a formal undead gala is perfectly in character. The deadpan delivery and mundane detail ('Which I made for the occasion') elevates it. Not exceptional but very much in the film's wheelhouse.

jokes.text: Jackie is introduced at the vampire-only party and declares 'I'm a vampire!' when questioned; she is not a vampire, she is Deacon's human servant
jokes.setup: The Unholy Masquerade is explicitly for the undead; a human is present and trying to pass
jokes.punchline: Jackie confidently insists twice 'I'm a vampire! I'm a vampire!' — clearly not one, with the comedic kicker that she was bitten by Nick and is now apparently undead, which also annoys Deacon since she was his servant
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Jackie has been turned — and that it was by Nick, not even Deacon after years of service — is a satisfying payoff. The doubled 'I'm a vampire!' has an improvised energy. Gets a solid laugh and sets up the next beat.

jokes.text: Deacon is visibly irritated that Nick turned his servant Jackie into a vampire without asking him, calling it 'pretty rude'
jokes.setup: Jackie has just revealed she is now a vampire, turned by Nick
jokes.punchline: Deacon's complaint is not about the ethics of vampirism or his servant's fate — it's the social impropriety of not being asked first. 'She was a pretty useless servant... yeah, but still, it would have been appreciated if you'd asked.'
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: first, Deacon's petty territorial complaint about not being consulted; second, his immediate admission she was 'pretty useless' anyway — undercutting his own grievance. This is tight character comedy. The structure is excellent — setup, undercut, persist — and it's very specific to Deacon's pompous, self-important personality.

jokes.text: 'How's Stu?' / 'He's good. He's here.' / 'Oh, he's here? Stu! STU!'
jokes.setup: In the middle of a conversation about vampire politics at an exclusive undead event, someone casually asks after Stu — the entirely normal human software analyst
jokes.punchline: The discovery that Stu is physically present at the monster party prompts immediate delight and shouting his name across the room, as though he's a beloved celebrity
jokes.explanation: Stu's status as the universally beloved normie in a world of monsters is one of the film's running conceits. The vampires' immediate pivot to warmly hollering his name across a gothic masquerade is a good beat. The joke is in the incongruity and the genuine affection.

jokes.text: 'Has anyone looked at you like they want to eat you, at all?' — asked of Stu upon arrival at the vampire party
jokes.setup: Stu arrives at a party full of vampires and other monsters who would naturally want to consume him
jokes.punchline: Instead of warning him, a vampire cheerfully asks if he's already been eyeballed as prey, as if checking in on a social experience
jokes.explanation: Very economical dark comedy. The casualness of the question — treating being eyed as food as a minor social inconvenience worth checking in on — is perfectly in the film's tone. Highly quotable and efficient.

jokes.text: The Unholy Masquerade MC announces they are raffling 'a live big pet' as the prize
jokes.setup: Formal society announcements at the Unholy Masquerade proceed like any community event raffle
jokes.punchline: 'We're raffling a live big pet this year' — clearly a live human or large animal for feeding — described with mundane raffle logistics: '$10 each or $45 for a book of five'
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of mundane community-event raffle language ('book of five') with the horrifying prize is a great deadpan joke. The specificity of the pricing is what sells it — it's the kind of detail that makes the gag feel improvised and real. Strong economy and originality.

jokes.text: Vladislav reveals 'The Beast' is actually his ex-girlfriend Pauline: 'The Beast is, uh, the name I gave to my ex-girlfriend Pauline. She prefers Pauline.'
jokes.setup: An ancient, powerful vampire dramatically refers to 'The Beast' — the established season-long mysterious antagonist — as the guest of honor
jokes.punchline: The Beast is just his ex-girlfriend Pauline, who understandably 'prefers Pauline', deflating the mythic menace instantly
jokes.explanation: This is one of the film's best jokes. The setup pays off a mythology-level mystery ('The Beast') with the most bathetic possible answer: a spurned girlfriend who has a reasonable preference about her name. 'She prefers Pauline' is the perfect economy punchline — three words that collapse the entire mystique. The character integration is superb: only Vladislav, with his outsized ego and romantic dysfunction, could have this backstory. The joke earns its 8+ because it simultaneously functions as a callback payoff, a character reveal, and a subversion of genre expectation, all in two sentences.

jokes.text: Vladislav describes his relationship with The Beast/Pauline: 'We were very... sexually explosive. Last time I saw her, she impaled me and called me an asshole.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav is describing their intense past relationship with apparent wistfulness
jokes.punchline: The 'sexually explosive' buildup pivots to being literally impaled on a lamp post while she called him an asshole — the mundane romantic grievance (name-calling) delivered while he was skewered on street furniture
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'sexually explosive' (which the audience might take as metaphor) to literal impalement is perfectly structured. The kicker — that what hurt most was being called an asshole while impaled — prioritizes emotional over physical pain in a very human way, making the supernatural absurdity poignant and funny simultaneously. 'All this while I was impaled on a lamp post' is a great button.

jokes.text: Reactions to the 'new guy' at the party — 'What, what kind of vampire... if he is a vampire. Did you see his face?'
jokes.setup: An unidentified vampire is spotted at the masquerade — apparently either very unusual-looking or not vampire at all
jokes.punchline: The flustered, uncertain reaction ('if he is a vampire') and focus on his face implies something spectacularly wrong about his appearance
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh, mostly setup for a visual gag we can't see in transcript. Weak without the visual.

jokes.text: Stu is introduced to vampires at the party; one immediately tries to feel his pulse: 'You got really warm hands too. You a demon?'
jokes.setup: Stu is introduced as a guest at the vampire party; a vampire shakes his hand
jokes.punchline: The vampire immediately clocks Stu's warmth (indicating a living human) and his best guess is 'demon?' — skipping the obvious 'human' conclusion entirely
jokes.explanation: Good economy — the vampire senses warmth and immediately leaps to supernatural explanations, never considering 'human' because humans simply don't attend these events. The logic is impeccable from a monster's perspective and plays well.

jokes.text: 'No, he's not a demon! I'm a software analyst.'
jokes.setup: A vampire has just asked if Stu is a demon based on his warm hands
jokes.punchline: Stu's perfectly calm correction — 'I'm a software analyst' — as though this is an entirely reasonable clarification at a monster party
jokes.explanation: One of Stu's defining moments — the joke is entirely in his unflappable calm. 'Software analyst' as a rebuttal to 'demon?' is a perfect comic non-sequitur delivered as pure sincerity. Stu's character is built on this exact joke type: the mundane stated with total equanimity amid supernatural chaos. Highly quotable, excellent economy, essential character moment.

jokes.text: Viago tries to explain Stu to other vampires: 'He's not vampire, or a zombie... He's not uh... he's neither, he's uh... more of a human.'
jokes.setup: Other supernatural beings are trying to categorize Stu at the monster party
jokes.punchline: 'More of a human' — as though 'human' is an unusual edge case requiring careful diplomatic phrasing rather than simply the default state of most beings
jokes.explanation: 'More of a human' is delightfully calibrated hedging — Viago can't quite bring himself to say the word directly, as though it's an embarrassing category. Classic Viago flustered politeness in the face of an awkward social situation.

jokes.text: 'Do you mind if Stu is killed?' — Nick is calmly asked whether his human friend can be eaten
jokes.setup: Nick has brought Stu to the vampire party and is now being approached about the matter
jokes.punchline: The question is phrased with the politeness of asking if someone minds the window being opened — 'Do you mind if Stu is killed?' — as though murder requires only mild social courtesy
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — the entire joke is in the phrasing. The horrifying request is delivered with exquisite politeness, and Nick's response ('I don't feel real good about it') matches the understatement perfectly. Very quotable standalone line.

jokes.text: A vampire asks Stu if he is 'predeceased' — using supernatural bureaucratic language to ask if he's dead
jokes.setup: Vampires are trying to establish whether Stu qualifies as an undead guest or is a living human (and therefore prey)
jokes.punchline: 'Are you, um... are you, are you, are you predeceased?' — the flustered, repeated 'are you' builds like a question too delicate to ask, and the word 'predeceased' reframes death as a mere bureaucratic status
jokes.explanation: 'Predeceased' is a genuinely clever euphemism — it's the kind of word you'd find in an estate lawyer's documents, applied here as polite supernatural parlance. The stuttering repetition also implies discomfort about asking, which adds to the comedy.

jokes.text: 'If anyone's gonna eat him it's gonna be us, but we're not, we're passed it. They can just go fuck themselves.'
jokes.setup: Other vampires are threatening to eat Stu; the main vampire flatmates try to defend him
jokes.punchline: Viago's defense is not 'Stu is off limits' but rather a possessive claim ('if anyone's gonna eat him it's us') immediately abandoned ('we're passed it') followed by genuine indignation on his behalf
jokes.explanation: The joke builds on the vampires' genuine affection for Stu coexisting with their predatory nature — they'd eat him if they could but they can't, so territorial pride and friendship occupy the same breath. The quick pivot from 'ours' to 'we're passed it' is a lovely self-aware moment. 'They can just go fuck themselves' as the conclusion is perfectly petty.

jokes.text: 'Nick! It is your fault. Okay? You brought a human into this den of vampis nest.'
jokes.setup: Nick is being blamed for bringing Stu to the vampire party
jokes.punchline: 'Den of vampis nest' — Deacon attempts a dramatic phrase but mangles 'den' and 'nest' into one confused compound, delivered with full conviction
jokes.explanation: The malapropism of 'den of vampis nest' is a fun bit of improvised language stumbling that feels authentic to Deacon's self-important bluster. Mild laugh, character-consistent.

jokes.text: 'He could be texting his mates, saying I've got them all under one place, come on over. We'll have a vampire barbecue!'
jokes.setup: Vampires debate whether Stu could be a vampire hunter scouting for an attack
jokes.punchline: The paranoid fantasy of Stu texting coordinates for a 'vampire barbecue' — the casual modern slang ('texting his mates') against the gothic horror scenario, plus 'barbecue' as the method of vampire destruction
jokes.explanation: Modern slang ('texting his mates') against the vampire paranoia context is a good contemporary fish-out-of-water gag. 'Vampire barbecue' is a nicely chosen word — barbecue implies sunlight, fire, the whole deal, reduced to a social event name.

jokes.text: 'Well, he's not, he's not doing that. He's wearing a bow-tie, look at him!'
jokes.setup: Vampires are debating whether Stu is a spy or hunter
jokes.punchline: Viago's decisive counter-evidence that Stu is not a threat: the bow-tie. As though bow-tie wearers cannot be vampire hunters.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Viago logic — his faith in Stu is total and his reasoning is entirely aesthetic. 'He's wearing a bow-tie, look at him!' is both specific to Viago's old-world gentility (he would trust a bow-tie) and wonderfully absurd as exculpatory evidence. Very quotable, great economy, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Stu introduces himself to the assembled vampires by explaining his job as a software analyst in great detail — describing business requirements analysis — while they wait for a reason not to eat him
jokes.setup: Stu has been asked to address the vampire assembly and justify his presence; everyone is waiting for something impressive
jokes.punchline: Stu explains, in careful corporate language, that he analyzes business requirements and builds software to fit them — a thorough, sincere, entirely unimpressive answer to beings who wanted to know if he was worth keeping alive
jokes.explanation: One of Stu's greatest moments — his complete earnestness in the face of an audience of bloodthirsty monsters who need convincing not to eat him, and the best he has is a GIS software explanation. The comedy is total and comes from his character: Stu is not performing, not panicking, just being himself. 'Don't fuck it up, man' and 'I can't hear Stu' amplify the tension. This earns its score for the sustained cringe-comedy and perfect character integration.

jokes.text: Stu's rambling explanation of his GIS software analyst job to a hall full of hungry vampires: 'We take like business requirements from organizations. Then we analyze those requirements and then we build software to fit those requirements.'
jokes.setup: Stu has been called upon to prove his worth to a vampire audience who wanted to eat him; his defense must be compelling
jokes.punchline: Stu's explanation is the most aggressively boring workplace description imaginable, delivered completely straight while his life hangs in the balance — the mundanity is the joke, as is the fact that it somehow might actually work
jokes.explanation: Extended cringe-comedy at its best. The setup — speak for your life — demands something remarkable; the punchline is the most unremarkable thing imaginable, stretched out for maximum discomfort. Stu's total obliviousness to the drama of the situation is perfect. The fact that it's genuinely accurate software-analyst-speak makes it funnier. High craft for a sustained comic beat.

jokes.text: 'He is a virgin. He is a virgin! I can smell a virgin of a thousand paces.'
jokes.setup: The vampires are unimpressed by Stu's software analyst credentials and are looking for reasons to spare or eat him
jokes.punchline: A vampire dramatically announces they can smell Stu's virginity — reframing his ordinariness as a prized quality in a grotesque way
jokes.explanation: Funny but slightly cheap — 'virgin' as vampire-prized quality is well-trodden folklore, and the joke leans on that mythology. 'A thousand paces' is a good detail. Gets a solid laugh.

jokes.text: 'Take your thousand paces and smell yourselves!'
jokes.setup: A vampire has just announced 'I can smell a virgin of a thousand paces'
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's comeback repurposes the 'thousand paces' boast as an insult: go back a thousand paces and smell yourselves
jokes.explanation: A precision comeback that reuses the exact language of the boast as a dismissal. The wordplay is tight — 'take your thousand paces and smell yourselves' inverts the boast perfectly. It's also a great character moment for Vladislav as the most aggressive and sharp-tongued of the flatmates. Very quotable, well-structured, great economy. Earns its score.

jokes.text: Vladislav fails to recognize his ex-girlfriend Pauline despite standing next to her — going through increasing guesses ('Georgie? No...') before getting it
jokes.setup: Pauline accuses Vladislav of forgetting her quickly; she was introduced earlier as his ex-girlfriend 'The Beast'
jokes.punchline: Vladislav genuinely cannot place her and runs through guesses: 'Georgie? No... not Georgie, like 5 years Saturday... Wait a minute. Just one moment. No... I've got it, it's coming...' — implying he has had so many lovers/enemies he can't track them
jokes.explanation: The joke is perfect character comedy — Vladislav is so ancient and so prolific in his feuds and romances that his own legendary nemesis/lover isn't instantly recognizable. 'Georgie? No, like five years Saturday' implies he has a Georgie he hasn't thought about in five years either. The long build ('I've got it, it's coming...') is excellent cringe-comedy timing.

jokes.text: 'Hello Beast.' / 'Hello asshole.' / 'Hey, don't call me asshole!' / 'Don't call me Beast.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav finally recognizes Pauline and greets her as 'The Beast'; she responds with her established grievance
jokes.punchline: The simultaneous mutual complaint — his nickname for her, her nickname for him — delivered as a mirrored argument that reveals they are essentially the same person
jokes.explanation: The parallel complaint structure — both simultaneously objecting to the other's nickname — is elegant and fast. It tells us everything about their relationship in four lines: mutually wounding, mutually unable to let go, perfectly matched in grievance. 'Hello asshole' as her first word to him is an excellent button. Very quotable exchange.

jokes.text: 'You know, the one who fucked the police...' — Pauline introduces herself to Vladislav's lover by referencing an apparently scandalous incident
jokes.setup: Pauline is being introduced to whoever Vladislav brought to the party
jokes.punchline: Her self-identifier is an apparent reference to some incident with police — delivered casually as a memorable distinguishing fact, with Vladislav immediately trying to shut it down ('Alright, that's old business')
jokes.explanation: A quick dark joke suggesting something historically scandalous between Vladislav and police — the deliberate vagueness and Vladislav's flustered dismissal make it funnier than any explicit explanation would. Good economy.

jokes.text: Vladislav: 'You will not feast on the blood of the human known as Stu.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav steps in to defend Stu from the assembled vampires
jokes.punchline: His heroic declaration is phrased in archaic vampire proclamation language: 'the human known as Stu' — combining his gothic register with Stu's completely ordinary name
jokes.explanation: 'The human known as Stu' is perfect — the grandiloquent legal/archaic phrasing around the most mundane possible name. It's also characteristically Vladislav: he can't help performing his own authority even in a crisis. A good, clean joke.

jokes.text: The antagonist vampire rants about cameras: 'This is a private secret society mate, you don't go bringing your bloody cameras into everything.'
jokes.setup: The documentary cameras are present at the secret vampire society gathering
jokes.punchline: A vampire — who has presumably been fine with cameras for the whole film — suddenly objects to them at the worst possible moment, adding a meta-layer of irony about the entire mockumentary premise
jokes.explanation: A quick meta joke that acknowledges the mockumentary conceit — this vampire is rightly baffled by the cameras' presence, which the main characters have seemingly normalized. Funny but not deeply developed.

jokes.text: 'You will not eat Stu and you will not eat the camera guy. Maybe one camera guy...'
jokes.setup: Vladislav is laying down protective rules for his friends and the documentary crew
jokes.punchline: He extends protection to the camera crew and then immediately carves out a possible exception — 'maybe one camera guy' — revealing that his altruism has limits and the crew are expendable in a pinch
jokes.explanation: The 'maybe one camera guy' exception is a perfect dark escalation — the protective declaration immediately hedged by genuine appetite. It's also a great meta-gag, acknowledging the camera crew's mortal peril. Excellent economy; the pause before 'maybe one camera guy' would be perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Full vampire brawl breaks out — 'Vampire fight! Get him Vladislav! Rip his head off!'
jokes.setup: Vladislav has challenged the antagonist vampire's threat with 'Well, what about this? Diego, rip his head off.'
