jokes.punchline: What was a tense standoff collapses into an apparently chaotic vampire brawl, with the crowd excitedly cheering ('Vampire fight!') like it's a sporting event
jokes.explanation: The escalation from tense negotiation to immediate violence is funny, and 'Vampire fight!' being shouted with genuine excitement plays like a schoolyard moment. Mostly a physical gag that works better on screen.

jokes.text: 'It is forbidden for vampires... to kill a vampire.' — announced during the brawl with a 'Medic!' immediately following
jokes.setup: A vampire has apparently just been severely injured or killed during the vampire fight
jokes.punchline: The solemn proclamation of an ancient rule is immediately undercut by someone shouting 'Medic!' — blending gothic vampire law with the banal logistics of a party injury
jokes.explanation: 'Medic!' after a vampire-on-vampire injury, alongside the solemn invocation of ancient law, is a good juxtaposition. The mundane shout against the gothic backdrop lands well.

jokes.text: Post-fight: 'We both, together, equally destroyed that guy! Yeah, but it was more Stu with the giant stick!'
jokes.setup: The vampire fight has apparently been won with Stu's unlikely assistance
jokes.punchline: Vladislav claims shared credit for the victory; Nick immediately corrects that it was mostly Stu — the quiet software analyst — who did the most damage with 'the giant stick'
jokes.explanation: Stu continuing to be the most effective and capable person in every situation is a great running gag. 'The giant stick' is specific and funny — not a dramatic weapon but improvised, practical, effective. Perfectly in character for Stu.

jokes.text: 'I hope this doesn't make this awkward for you and The Beast.' / 'No, I think it's opened up new possibilities.'
jokes.setup: They've just had a violent confrontation involving Vladislav's ex Pauline/The Beast
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's assessment that the violent chaos has 'opened up new possibilities' for their relationship — suggesting he finds their dysfunction romantic
jokes.explanation: Vladislav's romantic optimism about chaos and violence is very character-specific — this is exactly who he is, someone for whom impalement is foreplay. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'Stu, Stu, Stu, Stu! Stu, Stu, STU!' — the vampires collectively chant Stu's name, now being chased by werewolves
jokes.setup: The vampire party has descended into chaos; now werewolves are apparently chasing everyone
jokes.punchline: The vampires' response is to chant Stu's name like a war cry/sporting event chant as they run — Stu having become the collective mascot of the vampire house
jokes.explanation: The 'Stu' chant is a fun crowd energy gag — turning a chaos scene into a rally cry for the most ordinary person present. Works as an escalation and a running joke about Stu's beloved status.

jokes.text: Werewolves encounter — 'Look what the cat dragged in, huh?' / 'Piss off.' / 'Keep walking. Don't hassle us tonight.'
jokes.setup: The vampire group encounters werewolves — an established antagonistic relationship from earlier in the film
jokes.punchline: The vampire uses the idiom 'look what the cat dragged in' — a cat reference directed at someone who is literally about to become a wolf — without apparent awareness of the irony
jokes.explanation: The 'cat' idiom against werewolves is a nice touch — probably unintentional in-universe, which makes it funnier. The whole exchange is brisk and sets up the escalation to come.

jokes.text: 'Guys, where's your tracksuit pants?' / 'It was washing night. My misses couldn't wash them cause there was too much blood on them.'
jokes.setup: The werewolves are preparing for their monthly transformation and are without their usual tracksuit pants — which we know from earlier they wear to accommodate expanding legs
jokes.punchline: The logistical explanation — the trousers had too much blood on them from previous transformations to be washed in time — treats lycanthropy as a domestic inconvenience
jokes.explanation: The logistics of werewolf laundry — bloodstained trousers your wife couldn't wash in time for transformation night — is a beautiful mundane-meets-supernatural joke. It treats lycanthropy as the kind of monthly hassle that creates genuine domestic friction. 'My misses couldn't wash them' has real specificity and character. Earns its score for the richness of the mundane detail.

jokes.text: 'When your legs expand they go into the tracksuit. Those jeans are gonna rip completely!'
jokes.setup: The werewolves are wearing jeans instead of their transformation-appropriate tracksuit pants
jokes.punchline: Viago's concerned, almost parental worry about the werewolves' trouser situation — genuinely invested in whether their jeans will survive the transformation
jokes.explanation: Viago as the worried mum who can't help noting practical clothing problems even among enemy supernatural creatures is a perfect character beat. The genuine concern ('Those jeans are gonna rip completely!') is warmly funny.

jokes.text: 'Declan, that tree's far too thin! Look at it! It's like a branch! You don't know how big you get when you transform!'
jokes.setup: The werewolves are chaining themselves to trees in preparation for transformation
jokes.punchline: Viago can't help critiquing their tree selection — the chosen tree is too thin for the size they'll become, and Viago has apparently observed enough transformations to know
jokes.explanation: Viago's transformation into backseat werewolf prep coach is delightful. 'You don't know how big you get when you transform!' — said to an actual werewolf — is pure absurdist character comedy. The specificity of critiquing tree diameter makes it land.

jokes.text: Anton has forgotten the combination to his chain lock — and apparently set it to something other than 0000, the factory setting
jokes.setup: Werewolves are chaining themselves to trees for the full moon; Anton is fumbling with a combination lock
jokes.punchline: He forgot the combination — the existential silliness of a werewolf unable to chain himself up because he can't remember his own lock code, with Viago guessing 'it's probably four zeros, that's the factory setting'
jokes.explanation: The werewolf-forgot-his-lock-combination gag treats the monthly self-chaining ritual as pure bureaucratic hassle. 'Why did you get a combination lock? / I lost my key last time' is a perfect escalation — the solution to the previous problem has created a new one. The 'four zeros, factory setting' detail from Viago is exactly right.

jokes.text: 'Werewolves, not swearwolves.'
jokes.setup: A stressed werewolf preparing for transformation tells Viago to 'fuck off to a tree'
jokes.punchline: Viago gently corrects with the werewolf group's established catchphrase/rule: 'Werewolves, not swearwolves.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the entire film. 'Werewolves, not swearwolves' achieves something rare: a wordplay joke that is also deep character comedy. It's the perfect articulation of the werewolves' earnest, slightly dorky self-improvement culture — they're trying to be better than their baser nature. The pun itself is excellent (the wolf/wolf rhyme with the swap of 'swear-'). Perfectly economical — four words. Iconic, quotable, defines the werewolves as characters. This is the standard for 8+ in this reel.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, I know, well on transformation nights, it's alright, alright? I'm getting stressed out.' — the werewolf defends his swearing with a contextual exception
jokes.setup: Viago has just invoked 'werewolves, not swearwolves'
jokes.punchline: The werewolf immediately argues for a transformation-night exemption to the no-swearing rule — the earnestness of making an official exception to a self-imposed rule about the worst possible occasion to maintain it
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke — the werewolf is so stressed about transformation logistics that he's already lawyering around the group's core value. The logic is impeccable from his perspective and completely absurd. Good character follow-through.

jokes.text: Viago notices one of the werewolves is wearing fur: 'Is it fur? Oh, for crying out loud.' — a vampire is offended by a werewolf wearing animal fur
jokes.setup: The vampire Viago, who apparently has strong animal ethics, spots a werewolf wearing a fur coat
jokes.punchline: The irony that a werewolf — who literally transforms into a large fur-covered animal — is wearing animal fur as a fashion choice, and the vampire is the one offended by it
jokes.explanation: A nicely layered absurdist joke — Viago's ethical objection to a werewolf's fur coat is doubly ironic (werewolf, wearing fur, while about to become fur). 'That's disgusting, man. You're wearing fur.' being said by another supernatural predator adds the extra layer. 'That's not real fur' as a defense is a funny attempt at ethical mitigation from a werewolf.

jokes.text: Werewolf leader continues: 'I know, well on transformation nights it's alright, alright? I'm getting stressed out.'
jokes.setup: The swearwolves rule has been stated; the leader himself is now under pressure
jokes.punchline: The leader immediately qualifies his own rule — 'on transformation nights it's alright' — revealing the rule has exceptions, and then 'I'm getting stressed out' as a vulnerable admission mid-standoff undercuts his authority
jokes.explanation: Perfect follow-through on the swearwolves joke. The leader's immediate rule-exception undermines his own authority comedy — 'I'm getting stressed out' is a great vulnerability beat for the alpha of a werewolf pack. Good escalation.

jokes.text: 'Get that camera out of my face!' — a transforming werewolf objects to being filmed mid-transformation
jokes.setup: The werewolves are beginning to transform and the documentary cameras are present
jokes.punchline: Even mid-supernatural-transformation, the werewolf's response is a standard 'get that camera out of my face' — the kind of thing you'd hear from a celebrity, not a werewolf
jokes.explanation: Minor meta gag — works in context but not particularly original. Similar camera-objection beat was just done at 69:00.

jokes.text: The chase sequence: 'Run, Stu, RUN!' shouted over the chaos of a werewolf attack
jokes.setup: The werewolves have begun transforming and the group is fleeing
jokes.punchline: 'Run, Stu, RUN!' — the specific concern for Stu above all others in a life-threatening situation, echoing Forrest Gump but also just being exactly what everyone would shout
jokes.explanation: In context this is a good laugh — the vampires (who could fly or otherwise escape supernaturally) are most urgently concerned for the human. Simple but effective running-gag payoff.

jokes.text: In the attack's aftermath: 'Look away Nick! Don't look at their blood!' — warnings about blood triggering vampires, even in a traumatic scene
jokes.setup: The werewolves have apparently mauled someone (Stu) and blood is everywhere; Nick is in distress
jokes.punchline: Even in a moment of genuine horror and loss, Viago's practical vampire management concern — don't let Nick see blood or he'll frenzy — asserts itself, treating Nick's potential blood-lust as a parenting problem
jokes.explanation: Tonal comedy — the mundane vampire management concern in the middle of the horror. Works but doesn't quite land as a pure joke given the film's shift toward genuine emotion here.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'He's probably still a little upset having seen his best friend disemboweled by werewolves.' — delivered as clinical understatement about Nick
jokes.setup: Nick is clearly distraught after Stu's apparent death
jokes.punchline: 'Probably still a little upset' — the most staggering understatement for watching your best friend be disemboweled, delivered with Viago's characteristic gentle remove from human emotion
jokes.explanation: 'A little upset' for disembowelment is classic deadpan understatement and very Viago — he's so old and has seen so much death that his emotional calibration for human loss is permanently miscalibrated. Great economy.

jokes.text: Vladislav comforts the grieving Nick: 'But this is what happens when you are a vampire. You have to watch everyone die.'
jokes.setup: Nick has just lost Stu and is grieving; Vladislav sits beside him
jokes.punchline: What begins as genuine vampire wisdom pivots to a list of absurd death scenarios — 'like slipping and falling onto a giant spike. Or falling asleep in an autumn pile of leaves, and having some of them block your windpipe.'
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best sustained bits. Vladislav is delivering genuine vampire philosophy — the burden of immortality watching mortals die — but his examples reveal an ancient being who has accumulated millennia of bizarre and undignified death scenarios: spike-falls, leaf-blocked windpipes, duck attacks (masks made of crackers). The list escalates into pure absurdism while somehow remaining emotionally sincere. 'Fashioning a mask out of crackers and being attacked by ducks. Geese. Swans.' is a spectacular line. The specificity is extraordinary — he's clearly speaking from personal experience. Earns 8+ for the structural arc, character integration, and the cracker-mask detail which is genuinely one of the film's great lines.

jokes.text: Viago continues the death list: '...or making the simple mistake of fashioning a mask out of crackers and being attacked by ducks. Geese. Swans.'
jokes.setup: Viago is listing the ways his immortal friends have died over the centuries
jokes.punchline: The cracker-mask death by waterfowl is immediately the most absurd thing in the film — and then it's escalated through three birds (ducks → geese → swans) with ominous gravity, as if swans are the most fearsome endpoint
jokes.explanation: One of the great jokes in the film and in this reel. 'Fashioning a mask out of crackers and being attacked by ducks' is an absolutely original comedic image — specific, visual, completely unexpected. The escalation through 'geese' and finally 'swans' — delivered as the apex of waterfowl threat — is structurally perfect, with each additional bird adding gravity to the absurdity. Swans, specifically, are known to be aggressive, which makes the final beat land for attentive viewers. This is exactly the kind of joke that becomes a touchstone. Comparable to the highest-tier anchors in originality and structure.

jokes.text: 'Or simply dying of old age. But even old age is brutal. Watching your friends grow old. They can't piss. And they say stupid things and their brains go and they can't remember anything.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav continues his speech about the burdens of vampire immortality
jokes.punchline: The list of indignities of human old age — 'they can't piss, say stupid things, their brains go' — is both darkly funny and genuinely poignant; a vampire has watched centuries of people he loved deteriorate
jokes.explanation: This transitions from comedy to something genuinely affecting — the 'can't piss' detail is funny, but 'one day they can't even remember who you are / and you wish they were dead / and then they do die' is genuinely moving. The joke-to-pathos ratio here is unusual and effective. Good balance of dark comedy and actual character depth.

jokes.text: 'No. If I know Stu... this was probably the way he wanted to go. Disemboweled by werewolves. Blood and guts, splat onto the trees. His face torn to shreds.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav is trying to comfort Nick with a silver lining to Stu's death
jokes.punchline: His comforting thought: Stu probably WANTED to go this way — with graphic detail suggesting this is the ideal death by his estimation, described with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: The idea that a mild-mannered GIS software analyst's preferred death is werewolf disembowelment — presented as genuine comfort by an ancient vampire — is a perfect dark joke. The graphic specificity ('splat onto the trees, his face torn to shreds') as comforting eulogy detail is pitch-perfect absurdism.

jokes.text: 'I hope I made you feel better.' — Vladislav's conclusion after describing Stu's disembowelment in graphic detail as a comforting eulogy
jokes.setup: Vladislav has just delivered a speech listing every horrible way people die and concluding Stu wanted to be ripped apart
jokes.punchline: 'I hope I made you feel better.' — delivered with apparent sincerity as a coda to the most comically unhelpful eulogy imaginable
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the entire speech. 'I hope I made you feel better' caps a monologue that catalogued spike-falls, cracker-mask duck attacks, and werewolf disembowelment as 'comfort.' The gap between Vladislav's intent and his effect is the core character joke, delivered with maximum economy and sincerity. This is a great closer for a sustained bit.

jokes.text: Police talking heads: officers describe the werewolf attack as 'a pack of dogs' and reference 'dangerous dogs not being looked after'
jokes.setup: The aftermath of the werewolf attack is being investigated by police
jokes.punchline: The police are entirely convinced it was a large dog attack — 'more than just one' — and begin talking about responsible pet ownership and dog control, while presumably surveying the aftermath of a werewolf rampage
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary irony — official spokespeople explaining away supernatural events with the most mundane available explanation. The dog-attack framing and responsible pet ownership talk against what we know happened is a good sustained gag. 'These attacks have been happening on a monthly basis' is a beautiful clue hidden in officialspeak.

jokes.text: 'These attacks have been happening more, more frequent. They're happening on a monthly basis.' — police officer unknowingly describes the werewolf lunar cycle
jokes.setup: Police are discussing the 'dog attacks' occurring in the area
jokes.punchline: 'Monthly basis' — the officer has inadvertently cracked the case (full moon cycle) while talking about dangerous dogs
jokes.explanation: The 'monthly basis' detail is a layered joke — the officer is one clue away from the truth and doesn't know it. Rewards attentive viewers and plays even better on rewatch. Good economy.

jokes.text: Police officer has captured what he believes is the attack dog: 'I've got the bastard. One of them here, hey? That's what I'm talking about. Look at it. End of the day, this dog is gonna have to be put down.'
jokes.setup: Police are investigating the 'dog' attack; we hear an officer has captured the culprit
jokes.punchline: The 'dog' is implied to be a transformed (or transforming back) werewolf being treated as a regular dangerous dog — the officer's triumphant satisfaction about catching it makes the irony funnier
jokes.explanation: The triumphant police officer who has 'caught' a werewolf and plans to have it 'put down' as a dangerous dog is a solid visual/irony gag. 'Look at it. Look at what you did' — presumably to a person-sized 'dog' — lands well.

jokes.text: Vladislav talking head: 'They say that vampires' hearts are cold and dead. Definitely dead.' — pause — 'But I don't know. I think I still feel things inside it.'
jokes.setup: In the wake of Stu's death, Vladislav reflects on vampire emotion
jokes.punchline: He confirms the 'cold and dead' part without hesitation ('Definitely dead') and then pivots to a surprisingly sincere emotional admission, undermining the gothic pose with real feeling
jokes.explanation: 'Definitely dead' as the unambiguous confirmation, followed immediately by emotional vulnerability, is a good joke-structure pivot. Vladislav admitting to feelings while literally confirming his heart is dead is a nice existential beat. The pause between 'definitely dead' and 'but I don't know' would be perfectly timed.

jokes.text: 'Bye Stu. He would have loved his scarf. It was lovely, loose knit.'
jokes.setup: The vampires are mourning Stu at what appears to be a graveside or memorial
jokes.punchline: Viago's tribute to Stu focuses entirely on a scarf he apparently had for him — the gift going undelivered, described with the loving detail ('lovely, loose knit') of someone for whom textile craft is genuine emotional expression
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best jokes and a perfect character moment. Viago's grief manifests as concern about an undelivered scarf — specifically described as 'lovely, loose knit.' This is Viago entirely: genuinely caring, hopelessly domestic, expressing deep loss through craft. The specificity of 'loose knit' as the detail he lingers on is extraordinary. It's simultaneously funny and genuinely touching — the best kind of comedy. The character integration is exceptional; no other character in this film could deliver this line.

jokes.text: Deacon asleep in the wrong place: woken up with 'Deacon, wakey wakey! You don't sleep in here. The curtain's opened. It's nearly morning. You want to get sizzled to a crisp?'
jokes.setup: In the midst of grief and loss, Viago pivots to a domestic household issue
jokes.punchline: Deacon has fallen asleep somewhere exposed to sunlight — Viago's immediate pivot from grief to nagging about vampire safety hazards treats 'getting sizzled to a crisp' as a minor household inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Viago as the vampire housemother continues — 'you want to get sizzled to a crisp' as a mild domestic scold is a great line. The abrupt domestic pivot from mourning Stu to waking up the irresponsible Deacon is perfect rhythm comedy.

jokes.text: Stu is revealed to be alive — now a werewolf, bearing prominent scars: 'Look at his face! / Look! He looks like Seal!'
jokes.setup: Everyone believed Stu was dead; a text has arrived (shown at 78:34, 'Received at 4:20 AM') and they respond to find Stu is alive
jokes.punchline: He's survived but is now scarred by the werewolf attack, and someone immediately compares his new facial scars to the musician Seal — a very specific contemporary cultural reference that is both affectionate and absurd
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Stu alive is a genuine moment of joy, and 'He looks like Seal!' lands as a great comic observation — specific, contemporary, affectionate. Seal famously has facial scarring from lupus (a word derived from 'wolf'), which adds an extra layer of absurdist resonance probably intentional given the werewolf context.

jokes.text: Stu's account of waking up after the attack: 'And I woke up. And it was daytime. And I couldn't find my clothes.'
jokes.setup: Stu is recounting his experience of being attacked by werewolves, going into shock, and waking up
jokes.punchline: The list of post-transformation discoveries ends on 'I couldn't find my clothes' — the most mundane and practical of concerns after a near-death werewolf experience, delivered with Stu's characteristic calm
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Stu — having survived a werewolf attack and apparent death, woken up transformed, the detail he volunteers is not the supernatural transformation but the missing clothes. This is exactly who Stu is and the character integration is superb. Also circles back to the tracksuit pants joke (the werewolves know exactly this problem).

jokes.text: The werewolves who attacked Stu are now supporting him through his transformation: 'Those werewolf guys... eventually found me. And they had some, they like, lent me some pants.'
jokes.setup: Stu explains who helped him after the attack
jokes.punchline: The werewolves who disemboweled him found him and lent him some trousers — the attackers becoming carers, with the trouser-lending being the specific act of werewolf community support highlighted
jokes.explanation: Beautiful callback to the tracksuit pants running gag — the werewolves lend Stu pants because they know exactly the trouser problem he's facing. The attackers-becoming-supporters beats, combined with the pants being the specific form of support, is excellent narrative economy. The werewolves' community ethos (they help their own even if 'their own' was just made by attacking him) is also funny.

jokes.text: Stu: 'Yeah, these are the guys who, um, turned me into a werewolf.' — said in the same tone as 'these are the guys who lent me their car'
jokes.setup: Stu has been introducing the werewolves to the vampires; the two groups are on uneasy terms
jokes.punchline: Stu announces his werewolf transformation with zero affect — not 'they destroyed my life' or 'they cursed me' but a casual attribution, as if reporting who gave him a lift home
jokes.explanation: Perfect Stu joke. His total affectlessness about being turned into a werewolf — announced in the same register as mentioning a minor administrative fact — is exactly what his character has always been. The casualness is funnier than any dramatic reaction could be. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'You knit your own jersey? / Yes. / Oh, yeah? / I knit. / Is that the moon, or? / Yes.'
jokes.setup: The werewolves are visiting the vampire flat; Vladislav notices one's hand-knitted sweater
jokes.punchline: The werewolf knits — the domesticity of a werewolf's hobby, combined with confirming the moon motif on the jersey is intentional — delivered with quiet pride
jokes.explanation: Very economical character-building gag — 'I knit' says a lot about the werewolves' gentle-giant community and subverts the monster archetype. The moon motif confirmation is a nice deadpan follow-up. Well-deployed.

jokes.text: 'Please, don't, ah, don't lick anything or... pee on anything.'
jokes.setup: Werewolves are visiting the vampire flat for the first time
jokes.punchline: Viago's first request to his houseguests — not to lick or urinate on his belongings — treats the werewolves as politely as possible while acknowledging their tendencies
jokes.explanation: Perfect Viago — the phrasing is so polite and so specific ('don't lick anything or pee on anything') that it implies these are real concerns being handled diplomatically. The character integration is excellent: only Viago would phrase a 'no urinating on my furniture' request with this much grace. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'We were worried at first, you know, we thought 'Ooh, they are just going to urinate on everything.' But they actually are really polite and pretty clean.'
jokes.setup: The vampires reflect on having werewolves as houseguests
jokes.punchline: Vladislav's prejudicial fears about werewolf bathroom habits are pleasantly confounded — 'actually really polite and pretty clean' — delivered as though this is a genuine revelation about an entire species
jokes.explanation: A good xenophobia-subversion joke — the vampires' preconceptions about werewolves' hygiene are overturned. Plays nicely with the film's underlying theme of supernatural creatures having the same petty prejudices as human communities.

jokes.text: Vladislav: 'There was obviously that werewolf smell, which permeated the entire house for the first half an hour. But we opened some windows and got rid of that.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav is reporting on the werewolf housevisit experience
jokes.punchline: He diplomatically acknowledges the werewolf smell but notes the ventilation solution — treating the supernatural stench as a minor hosting inconvenience resolved by an open window
jokes.explanation: Functional observational gag — the domestic solution to a supernatural problem. Good character voice for Vladislav but not exceptional on its own.

jokes.text: Werewolf alpha male: 'What a stupid suggestion, their idea,' I thought. No way. You know, walking into the vampire's den. That's ludicrous. That's my hand.'
jokes.setup: The werewolf leader is explaining why he decided to bring his pack to the vampire flat
jokes.punchline: 'That's my hand' — in the middle of a posturing alpha-male explanation, he suddenly notices his own hand on camera and momentarily loses his train of thought, completely deflating the speech
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best improvisational moments. The alpha male is building to a macho 'I made the call' speech when he suddenly gets distracted by his own hand appearing in frame and says 'That's my hand.' — perfectly natural, completely accidental-feeling, devastating in its comedic timing. This is what great mockumentary improvisation looks like. The deflation of the alpha pose by his own hand-awareness is brilliant.

jokes.text: 'I'm the alpha male. So, generally... all of the other guys follow me.'
jokes.setup: The werewolf leader is explaining the pack hierarchy
jokes.punchline: 'All of the other guys follow me' — delivered with uncertain conviction, as though he's not entirely sure this is still true or needs reassuring
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'I'm the alpha male' has increasingly diminishing self-conviction. Saying 'generally... all of the other guys follow me' is not what a truly confident alpha says. Good character work.

jokes.text: Toast: 'For Stu!' / 'For STU!' — werewolves and vampires united in a toast to their shared human friend
jokes.setup: Former enemies (vampires and werewolves) are now in the same living room as guests
jokes.punchline: Their only point of unity is their shared affection for Stu — the most ordinary human imaginable — who has effectively united two supernatural rival factions
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to Stu's function in the film. The idea that a software analyst from Wellington can unite vampires and werewolves is a beautiful absurd concept delivered simply.

jokes.text: 'For Stu!' / 'For STU!' — werewolves toast with beers in the vampire flat
jokes.setup: The vampire-werewolf meeting resolves in a moment of communal warmth
jokes.punchline: The toast is 'For Stu' — the entirely ordinary human software analyst is the totem around which ancient supernatural enemies unite
jokes.explanation: The 'For Stu' toast is a warm and funny convergence of the film's themes — the supernatural world repeatedly finds its humanity (or humanity-equivalent) through one ordinary NZ bloke. Well-earned payoff.

jokes.text: 'What have you done to your face?' / 'I got attacked by some werewolves.' — Stu's scarred face noted by a confused bystander
jokes.setup: Stu appears with severe facial scarring from his werewolf encounter
jokes.punchline: Stu's explanation — 'I got attacked by some werewolves' — is stated with the same casual tone he'd use for 'I had a minor accident' — total equanimity about a near-death transformation
jokes.explanation: A great Stu character moment — his matter-of-fact 'I got attacked by some werewolves' as a facial explanation is perfect deadpan. The 'some' in 'some werewolves' is a specifically Stu-ish qualifier. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'Army is a werewolf. Seemed like a very nice person.' — a talking head observation about a werewolf guest
jokes.setup: Viago is reflecting on meeting the werewolves
jokes.punchline: 'Seemed like a very nice person' — Viago's characteristically gentle assessment of a werewolf, treating being a werewolf as a biographical detail rather than a defining characteristic
jokes.explanation: 'Army is a werewolf. Seemed like a very nice person.' captures Viago's social generosity perfectly — the werewolf identity is noted and immediately set aside in favor of a character judgment. Very Viago.

jokes.text: Vladislav and his new vampire girlfriend Katherine: 'Some people freak out a bit about the age difference. They think, what's this 96-year-old lady doing with a guy four times her age.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav has found a new girlfriend Katherine and they discuss their relationship
jokes.punchline: The 'age difference' concern: Katherine is 96 and Vladislav is roughly 400+ — framing the criticism as 'cradle-snatching' when the 'young one' is a 96-year-old woman
jokes.explanation: The 'cradle-snatcher' framing applied to a 96-year-old is a great inversion — the joke recontextualizes the concept of a 'young woman' through the lens of vampire centuries. 'Who cares, they can call me a cradle-snatcher' said about a 96-year-old is excellent. Good character integration for Vladislav's total lack of self-awareness.

jokes.text: Vladislav and Pauline tentatively reunite: 'Pauline and I are tentatively back together. But it's not long before you remember why it was we broke up in the first place.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav reports on his relationship status after the events of the masquerade
jokes.punchline: The talking head acknowledges they've gotten back together while simultaneously implying it's already a disaster — 'it's not long before you remember why' — delivered with weary inevitability
jokes.explanation: A structural joke that relies on our accumulated knowledge of Vladislav and Pauline — the inevitability is funny but not exceptional as a standalone gag. Functions as a setup for the following scenes.

jokes.text: Pauline orders household modifications: 'We start in our bedroom, and I need that totally boarded up or blacked out somehow.' / 'My husband is my familiar. So there has been a dynamic shift there.' / 'You could buy a Bedazzler. So you write that down. That's B-E-D...'
jokes.setup: Pauline has moved in with Vladislav and is immediately reorganizing his life
jokes.punchline: Three rapid-fire jokes: she's redecorating for vampire purposes; her human husband has been demoted to 'familiar' (and she notes the 'dynamic shift' with magnificent understatement); and she's spelling out 'Bedazzler' for someone taking notes
jokes.explanation: Three distinct funny moments compressed: Pauline immediately taking over Vladislav's space, the casual demotion of her human husband to familiar ('dynamic shift'), and the Bedazzler specification being spelled out. 'Dynamic shift' is particularly good understatement.

jokes.text: Vladislav: 'But I am your Master. Okay? / Yeah.' — immediately following professing love
jokes.setup: Vladislav and Katherine have just said 'I love you' to each other
jokes.punchline: He immediately appends 'But I am your Master. Okay?' — unable to let a tender moment pass without asserting supernatural dominance
jokes.explanation: Perfect character moment — Vladislav literally cannot let 'I love you' be the last word without reasserting his Master status. Katherine's quiet 'Yeah' is the ideal response. This is exactly who Vladislav is.

jokes.text: Vladislav tests his familiars' laughter — checking who's actually laughing at his jokes, with spot-checks: 'What are you laughing at, Justin? Hey? What are you laughing at now? / Just then? / Yeah, yeah, but what? / Oh, I don't know. / Ah, test failed! Test failed!'
jokes.setup: Vladislav boasts that his familiars are required to laugh at all his jokes, and he tests them
jokes.punchline: He runs rigorous spot-checks on individual familiars to verify authentic laughter — 'You laughing? What are you laughing at now?' — the insecurity beneath the Master persona on full display, with 'Test failed!' as the verdict
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best character comedy sequences. Vladislav's familiar-laughter audit reveals the core joke of his character: the need for validation from people who are compelled to give it, making the validation worthless, which he then tries to verify — an impossible loop. 'Test failed!' for not being able to explain what you were laughing at is simultaneously petty and deeply sad. The question 'What are you laughing at Stu?' with 'I was laughing with the group / Yep, that's good' is a perfect button. Strong character integration, great structure.

jokes.text: 'You're laughing now. What are you laughing at now though? I don't know cause... Ah, another failure!' — the testing continues; Stu is then tested and passes by saying 'I was laughing with the group.'
jokes.setup: Vladislav's laugh-testing regime has claimed one failure (Justin)
jokes.punchline: The second failure confirms the pattern; Stu's answer ('laughing with the group') is accepted — 'Yep, that's good. That's good, yeah. Just pay attention. Pay attention. Laugh with the group.' — Stu's social instincts, even as a werewolf, remain perfectly calibrated
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the testing sequence: Stu passing the test with 'I was laughing with the group' — the most group-conformist possible answer — is perfect. Vladislav's satisfied 'yep, that's good' and instruction to 'laugh with the group' is a great button.

jokes.text: 'You will not remember the last hour and a half of what you have just seen. You will forget... the contents of this movie.'
jokes.setup: The film is ending; Vladislav addresses the camera directly
jokes.punchline: He attempts to mesmerize the audience into forgetting the entire film — the standard vampire mind-wipe trick applied to the fourth wall, suggesting the documentary's protective mechanism is a vampire power used on the viewing audience
jokes.explanation: A very elegant meta-joke to close the film. The vampire mind-wipe as the mechanism by which the documentary's subjects protect their secret — applied to the entire cinema audience — is both thematically resonant and funny. It retroactively explains how vampires could allow a documentary to exist. The specificity of 'the last hour and a half' (the film's runtime) is a lovely detail. Well-structured closing gag.
